title: [Netflix] Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
summary: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick ParkerYou click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.The cost of good neighborsMulti-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management.These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota.A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota.We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised the floor for everyone on the platform, and we are continuing that work.A decade of shared-kernel isolation, at Netflix and across the industry, has not made co-tenancy invisible, because a noisy neighbor is not one problem but a family of them. Almost every physical resource a host shares is its own axis of interference, and a cgroup can fence very few of them:CPU performance indeterminacy. Co-located threads contend for the run queue, so scheduling latency rises even while a container remains within its CPU quota. Separately, a neighbor with a large working set evicts a tenant’s last-level cache lines and saturates memory bandwidth, neither of which a CPU share can partition.Network bandwidth and packets per second. Per-container shaping competes for link bandwidth, and receives processing runs in softirq context, charging one container’s packet work to whatever CPU a neighbor is running on. A flood of small packets exhausts a core’s softirq budget long before any bandwidth cap is reached.Storage bandwidth and IOPS. A neighbor saturating a device’s queue serializes everyone’s I/O, and on cloud block storage, the per-volume and per-instance throughput ceilings are a shared budget in their own right.Long tail. Page-cache reclaim, NUMA and cross-socket interconnect traffic, TLB-shootdown interrupts, PCIe and GPU contention, package-level power and thermal throttling, and contention on kernel global locks (the class of problem behind Mount Mayhem) each degrade neighbors in their own way.What unites them is that they are physical, shared, and below the level a quota can reach. A platform can cap how much CPU time or memory a container is granted; it cannot hand each tenant its own slice of the memory bus, its own softirq budget, or its own portion of the last-level cache.Of these, the network dimension has bitten hardest in our experience. Per-container bandwidth shaping uses a hierarchical token bucket (HTB) queueing discipline that serializes traffic with a global lock to account for each container’s bytes and packets. Under a flood of small packets from a single container, contention for that lock can burn kernel CPU and starve co-located containers of the time they need to process their own traffic, resulting in TCP retransmits and tail-latency spikes on services that did nothing wrong. The mechanism meant to prevent noisy neighbors becomes one.The workloads most exposed to this are stateful, high-throughput streaming jobs: real-time data pipelines and stream processors that continuously move large volumes of data and maintain in-memory state. When one of these is perturbed, recovery is not cheap. A stream processor that falls behind or loses its place may have to restore from a checkpoint and pause processing for many minutes to catch up. For these jobs, intermittent interference from a neighbor is not a small slowdown that averages out; it is a stop-the-world event that pages an on-call engineer. The same teams report, accurately, that they never saw this on a plain EC2 instance.Why we kept coming back to the VMFull VM isolation, where a workload gets its own host and kernel, is the standard our customers are already happy with. The question was not whether VM isolation works; it was how to offer it without giving up what makes Titus worth using. We weighed four paths.Keep improving shared-kernel isolation. This helps every workload on the platform, needs no opt-in, and we are still investing in it (more on the roadmap below). Its limitation is structural. Each round of tuning narrows the gap without closing it, because the underlying hardware remains shared. Cache, memory bandwidth, and the kernel’s own shaping and scheduling locks are not things a container boundary can fully contain. Shared-kernel isolation is the right default and the wrong promise for a workload that cannot tolerate a bad minute.microVMs (Firecracker, Kata Containers). Lightweight VMs boot in about 150 milliseconds by emulating far less hardware than traditional VMs, which is why they power serverless platforms. They were the most appealing alternative on paper, and we carefully reviewed them. Three things made the cost hard to justify. First, the hardware virtualization they rely on is available only on bare-metal instances or through nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on the instance types we run at Netflix at the time, so adopting microVMs broadly would have constrained us to a narrow slice of the fleet. Second, there is no managed microVM service we could build on, which means we would have to run and maintain a virtualization layer ourselves: patching the hypervisor, live-migrating guests, and qualifying emulated devices. That is exactly the kind of operational surface we prefer not to own when we can avoid it. Third, even setting those aside, microVMs add virtualization overhead on CPU- and IO-bound work and do not support GPUs. Excellent isolation, but at a price in flexibility and operational load we were not willing to pay.gVisor. A user-space kernel that intercepts system calls provides sandbox-grade isolation without a hypervisor, thereby avoiding the bare-metal constraint. The catch is performance and dependency. Intercepting syscalls in user space adds overhead on IO-heavy paths, which are precisely the workloads we most need to protect, and the open-source project lags behind its internal counterpart in fixes and is effectively maintained by a single vendor. The isolation we would gain came with a throughput tax on the exact jobs we were trying to help.Move the workload to EC2. It is possible to run containers directly on EC2 instances. The problem is that the application team takes back the operational load that Titus exists to carry: choosing instance types, patching hosts, and sizing and scaling the fleet. For a team that came to Titus precisely to avoid those things, this is a regression in the experience, and the move between Titus and EC2 has historically been a one-way door that teams are reluctant to cross.Spectrum of isolation options from lighter and more shared to stronger isolation: shared-kernel containers, then gVisor, then microVMs (Firecracker or Kata), then a full VM as used by single-tenant Titus, which is highlighted. Each option is annotated with its launch latency, overhead, and the entity that operates it; single-tenant Titus is a dedicated EC2 instance with no additional virtualization overhead.There is also a question of what kind of isolation we actually need. microVMs and gVisor are built for security isolation between mutually distrusting tenants, the case where one tenant might actively try to attack or escape into another. Among Netflix teams, that threat model is more than the situation warrants. What these workloads need is resource and performance isolation: a guarantee that a neighbor cannot steal their CPU, cache, memory bandwidth, or network, not protection from a hostile co-tenant. A dedicated EC2 VM delivers exactly that, with hardware we do not have to emulate and a kernel we do not have to sandbox. We pay for the isolation we need rather than for a stronger security boundary.microVMs and gVisor asked for a large, bespoke investment with real risk in order to approximate something we could get directly: a VM. Using EC2 to run containers provides the VM, but takes away the managed experience. So we took the direct route and brought single-tenant VM isolation into Titus itself, under the existing API and the existing shared-responsibility model.How single-tenant Titus worksThe idea is simple to state: a single-tenant task runs on its own EC2 instance, sized to fit it, with nothing else scheduled alongside. That instance is still a Titus container host that the Compute/Platform team owns and patches. The team running the workload sees the same Titus API and the same deployment path. Nothing about how they package or ship the job changes.Side-by-side anatomy of a multi-tenant Titus, where multiple teams’ containers share one Linux kernel and the hardware beneath it and contend with one another, versus a single-tenant node where one task plus its platform sidecars owns the whole machine with no co-tenants.Most of the work happens in the federation layer, the part of Titus that decides where a job runs (which cell, which capacity) before it is scheduled onto a node.When a job is eligible for single tenancy, three things happen.Federation decides eligibility and the envelope. Eligibility is governed by an allowlist maintained by the Compute/Platform team; a team opts in by targeting a single-tenant workload group rather than flipping a flag in the public API. For an eligible task, federation tags it as single-tenant and records the set of instance families it may run on, ensuring consistent performance across the workload. Consolidating this decision in federation follows the same principle we use for routing in general: placement intelligence belongs in one place, above the individual cells, where it can account for capacity and availability across the region.Autoscaling provisions a dedicated node. Given a pending single-tenant task, our autoscaling implementation launches the smallest instance that satisfies the task’s requested CPU, memory, and GPU from the allowed families for the task just in time. Taking the tightest fit keeps the unused remainder of each dedicated node small. The next section covers this in detail.The scheduler enforces one task per node. Single-tenant pods are configured with pod anti-affinity to prevent colocation with other pods, along with a priority class that exempts the task from preemption. Single-tenant nodes are also tainted to prevent unrelated workloads from being placed there, with only single-tenant workloads tolerating this taint. We also disable defragmentation/repacking for these nodes, so a single-tenant task is never relocated to repack the fleet. Together, these mean a single-tenant task has its host to itself for its entire life, undisturbed by a neighbor or by the platform’s own bin-packing.Two design choices are worth dwelling on. First, single tenancy is allowlisted on purpose. If it were a free checkbox in the API, most teams would tick it, because who wouldn’t want a quieter host? And the efficiency that multi-tenancy exists to provide would erode across the fleet. Keeping the Compute/Platform team in control lets us direct dedicated isolation to workloads that need it and steer the rest toward shared capacity, while keeping the public API surface small as we learn. Second, we do not silently resize anyone’s job to fill its node. The job keeps the resources it requested; we recommend sizing it close to a node shape so the dedicated instance is well utilized, while keeping the workload portable and running identically whether in single-tenant mode or not, regardless of the host’s dimensions. Moving in and out of the mode is a configuration change, not a rewrite.A few perpetrators, a lot of collateral damageNoisy-neighbor pain is not spread evenly. In practice, a small number of workloads cause most of the disruption: a job that floods the host with small packets, churns the page cache, or saturates memory bandwidth degrades the performance of every other container unlucky enough to share its host. Some of these are also among the workloads most affected by contention, because a job can be both a source of interference and sensitive to it. The shape of the problem is a few perpetrators and many victims.That shape is what makes single tenancy a precise lever rather than a blunt one. We do not need to give every workload its own machine. We need to pull the handful of perpetrators and the most disruption-sensitive victims onto dedicated nodes. Doing so protects their former neighbors directly and removes the reason the platform was spreading sensitive workloads apart with anti-affinity placement in the first place. The hosts left behind are quieter, and because they no longer have to be kept partly empty to honor spread rules, they pack more densely.Before-and-after view of the Titus fleet. Before: a few red perpetrators are scattered across shared hosts, the amber workloads beside them are disrupted, and anti-affinity spreading leaves dashed stranded capacity. After: each perpetrator runs on its own dedicated single-tenant node, the remaining shared hosts are fully loaded with healthy workloads, and one host’s worth of capacity is reclaimed.On the left is the fleet before: perpetrators sit on shared hosts, the workloads next to them suffer, and anti-affinity rules leave gaps that cannot be filled. On the right is the same fleet after: each perpetrator has its own right-sized node where it can be as noisy as it likes, with no one to disturb; the remaining hosts run full of undisturbed workloads; and the capacity that used to be stranded comes back. A few dedicated nodes buy isolation for the perpetrators and a calmer, denser fleet for everyone else.Provisioning many small nodesSingle tenancy trades fewer large, shared instances for more small, dedicated ones, and that shift has consequences across the stack.The first is the control-plane load. More nodes mean more for the Titus control plane to track and more VM launches against the EC2 control plane, the latter mattering most during a regional failover, when we scale up the fastest and can least afford a throttle. Titus is already a federated system: each region is divided into independent cells, which limit how large any single control plane can get, and let us add capacity by adding cells rather than growing a single stack without limit. We migrate workloads in stages rather than all at once, and we exercise the launch-rate path under controlled load on a schedule rather than discovering its limits during an incident.The second consequence is capacity management, where the design changed the most. With one task per node, the fleet now spans many instance shapes whose demand shifts continuously as jobs come and go. Pre-staging static pools of every shape would be slow to manage and wasteful, so we instead provision single-tenant nodes on demand. It handles provisioning end-to-end, and several of its features line up with exactly what single tenancy needs:Just-in-time, right-sized provisioning. Single-tenant jobs are configured with a list of supported instance families based on their performance requirements. At launch, they are mapped to the best-fit node size by comparing requested resources against the selected instance families. New nodes of that instance type are brought up by the autoscaler to meet the pending demand. Single-tenant pods are configured with anti-affinity to all other pods, so the scheduler naturally lands one pod per autoscaled node. Newly vacated nodes may be reused by any pending deploys before they’re automatically torn down. The node pools themselves are shared across single-tenant workloads and describe a catalog of available instance families and sizes.Single tenant node pools. Single tenant may run in separate clusters or be shared with multitenant clusters. The pools are configured with a list of supported instance-type permutations and are pinned to a Titus container host AMI. This is where the managed experience lives: the host image and its configuration are ours, declared once and applied to every node created.Consolidation management. In multi-tenant environments, we default to a repack/defrag behavior that periodically relocates workloads. This doesn’t apply in single tenant, where nodes are explicitly each running at most one workload. We therefore reclaim only nodes vacated by workloads that have scaled in or terminated. Node termination is performed in two stages, allowing nodes to be reused for pending workloads before they are fully terminated.Drift-based patching. When we publish a new container host AMI, we support a “mutable” deploy to existing nodes without affecting any hosted containers, and an “immutable” deploy that updates the target AMI for newly created nodes. This means that many node upgrades don’t require disrupting workloads, but we reserve the right to roll the fleet with our users if needed.The launch-latency tax, and why warm pools are harder hereProvisioning on demand does not make a node appear instantly, and launch latency is the tradeoff single tenancy asks us to manage most carefully. Bringing a single-tenant task to the point where it can serve traffic has two parts: standing the node up (booting a fresh EC2 instance, then pulling and extracting the container image, which is the largest part of host setup for most jobs) and the application’s own startup (a JVM loading and JIT-compiling its classes, a cache filling, and so on). A fresh instance takes tens of seconds before the image pull even begins.In multi-tenant Titus, most of this is hidden. A new task usually lands on a Titus container host that is already running and already has the image layers cached, so starting it takes only a few seconds rather than minutes; the host boot was paid for once, long ago, and amortized across every task that has run there since. Single tenancy gives up that hiding place. Every single-tenant task waits for its own machine to boot and pull its image.The usual remedy is a warm pool: keep some instances booted and idle so a pending task lands on one immediately. This works well for the multi-tenant fleet precisely because that fleet is close to homogeneous. A handful of large shapes cover almost everything, since any task can be packed onto a big shared host. A small amount of warm capacity in a few shapes gives a high hit rate, and its cost is spread across the many tasks that will use it.Single tenancy inverts those economics, and this is the part worth being explicit about.Press enter or click to view image in full sizeBecause every task gets a right-sized node, the fleet spans many instance shapes (several families across many sizes), and a warm instance only helps a pending task whose shape matches it. A warm r7i.2xlarge does nothing for a task that needs an m7a.8xlarge. To achieve a good hit rate, we would need to hold idle capacity in every family-and-size bucket, and idle capacity in a bucket with no task to fill is pure cost. The very property that makes single tenancy efficient at steady state, tight best-fit sizing, works against warm-pool reuse: more distinct shapes mean more buckets and a lower hit rate per dollar of standing capacity. And the pressure peaks exactly when it is least welcome. During a regional failover or a live event, when many tasks need fresh nodes at once, a thin warm pool spread across many shapes drains immediately, and the rest of the demand pays the full cold-boot cost.So we treat warm capacity as a small, targeted lever rather than a default. We keep a little pre-warmed capacity for the most latency-sensitive single-tenant starts, and we deliberately narrow the menu of shapes to a curated set of sizes rather than the full continuum, so warm capacity concentrates into fewer buckets and trades a little best-fit efficiency for a better hit rate. Everything else provisions just-in-time and accepts the boot.The more durable wins are in cutting the launch cost itself rather than pre-paying for it, and they help both single- and multi-tenant nodes, which is the better place to spend the effort:Faster image distribution. The image pull dominates the host setup, so newer OCI image formats and lazy-pulling snapshotters such as stargz and SOCI, which fetch only the bytes a container actually reads at startup rather than the whole image up front, reduce the largest component of the gap.Checkpoint and restore. For processes that are slow to initialize, snapshotting a warmed-up application with a tool like CRIU and restoring it, rather than cold-starting it, removes most of the second half of launch latency.Instance type selection. In multitenant configurations, we have historically used metal instances, which offer slightly better performance but come with a slower startup time. In a single-tenant configuration, node startup latency is more important, so we have moved away from these instances.Scheduling optimization. Through regular stress testing of fleet scaling, we found a scheduling bottleneck caused by Kubernetes preemption logic, leading to nodes being scaled up quickly but then left idle while waiting for workloads to be scheduled on them. This was ultimately unnecessary, as our single-tenant pools do not run preemptible workloads. Disabling preemption greatly improved scheduling performance when under strain.None of this makes the tradeoff disappear, and it is worth stating plainly: a single-tenant node is slower to stand up than a slot on an already-warm shared host, and hiding that with warm pools costs more per node here than it does on the multi-tenant fleet, because the warm pool cannot be as homogeneous. But for the long-running services that single tenancy targets, paying that cost once at launch in exchange for a quiet life afterward is a trade these teams are glad to make.Measuring the differenceIsolation claims are easy to assert and hard to trust, so we measure them with a repeatable benchmark and a single score.The method is a differential one. We run a reference container, a healthy and representative application, and record its throughput and tail latency while it runs alone. Then we run it again next to a havoc container engineered to be a bad neighbor: a UDP flood through XDP to stress the network-shaping path, pointer-chasing and STREAM to pollute the last-level cache and saturate memory bandwidth, fsync storms against the disk, stress-ng to abuse the scheduler, and GPU-burn to monopolize an accelerator. We only trust a run once the host has reached a steady state, which we confirm with the kernel’s Pressure Stall Information: we wait until cpu_some or mem_some shows that tasks are actually stalling on a contended resource, not merely that the resource is busy. Each scenario is run many times with fixed seeds, and we report the median with a bootstrapped confidence interval, because noisy-neighbor distributions are heavy-tailed and a simple average can mask the spikes that matter.From the reference container’s numbers, we derive a simple measure of how well isolation held. Throughput efficiency is the fraction of operations per second the app retains under attack; latency efficiency is the ratio of its undisturbed P99 to its P99 under pressure. A neighbor that doubles the reference app’s P99 drops the latency efficiency. As an illustration, a reference app whose P99 latency goes down next to a havoc container achieves a certain latency efficiency, and one whose throughput falls from a to b operations per second achieves a certain throughput efficiency. The composite score is a weighted blend of the two, with a latency-sensitive preset that gives greater weight to tail latency for interactive and streaming-path services. A perfectly isolated system scores 100%, and a single hard failure invalidates the run regardless of the average.Noisy-neighbor isolationcgroups container isolation isn’t perfect, and applications may experience worse performance due to sharing a machine with a determined neighbor. This could extend to disk and/or network IO where the same volumes or interfaces may be shared across workloads. For a distributed workload, this can lead to measurable inconsistencies in performance depending on where the replicas are placed. For more sensitive workloads, this variance can mean the difference between stability and getting paged.The single-tenant option makes it possible to better isolate workloads that cause problems for their neighbors and/or are more sensitive to such problems. This can be used as a stopgap until the specific regression problem is resolved and consistency is restored, or kept permanent for load patterns that aren’t worth supporting in a shared environment.EfficiencyThe second effect is fleet efficiency, and it is the one people expect to go the wrong way. Dedicating a node to a single task consumes that node’s slack, so the naive expectation is that utilization falls. In aggregate, it can move the other way, for a reason related to how we dealt with poor isolation before single tenancy existed.To protect sensitive workloads on shared hosts, the platform used anti-affinity placement, scattering them across the fleet to reduce colocation of the same workload on the same nodes. Spreading fights bin-packing: it strains capacity, because a host kept partly empty to honor an anti-affinity rule cannot be filled by a workload that would otherwise have fit there. When isolation-sensitive workloads move to dedicated nodes, the need for spreading and fragmentation goes away, and the remaining multi-tenant fleet can pack more densely.Another source of fragmentation is services that are sensitive to disruption. These are typically stateful services where recovery is expensive. As these services become more common in a given population, they can lead to nodes being held up by pods with strict disruption requirements. This can lead to an inability to defrag and recompact the pool during off-peak times. The symptoms and resulting drop in fleet efficiency caused by disruption-sensitive workloads mirror what’s observed for workloads with anti-affinity rules.Depending on the magnitude of the anti-affinity and/or disruption budget problem, moving such workloads to single-tenant pools can result in equivalent or even improved placement when all costs have been accounted for. It also becomes easier to quantify the cost to end-users. Rather than trying to attribute fleet-wide fragmentation to individual workloads, we can directly quantify waste as single-tenant node overhead.The theory and the practice diverge here, and it was the practice that decided it. In principle, the efficiency ceiling is higher for multi-tenant bin-packing: pack enough tasks together, and a host fills almost completely. We do not reach that ceiling. AWS offers a discrete set of instance sizes, so a large shared host rarely matches the exact sum of the requests we place on it, and the gap between a host’s capacity and what we can actually pack onto it is a bin-packing hole we cannot fill. At the granularity of large instances, those holes are sizable. Right-sizing an instance to a single workload, picking the closest fit from many shapes instead of draping many workloads over one big host, captured more of the available efficiency in our experience than the higher theoretical ceiling ever delivered. The clean theory favored multi-tenancy; our measured fleet favored right-sizing.Container-host maintenanceThe third effect is operational, and it shows up in how we keep the fleet patched. A multi-tenant host is hard to take down for maintenance precisely because it is full: draining it means relocating many tenants at once, several of which carry disruption budgets that limit how fast they can move, so a routine patch becomes a careful, coordinated evacuation. A single-tenant host runs exactly one task, with consolidation and defragmentation turned off, so draining it means relocating only the one workload, and we can automatically handle that when a new AMI ships. The remaining multi-tenant hosts are easier to maintain, too, because the workloads that were most sensitive to disruption are no longer stranded on them.What it changes, and what it doesn’tSingle-tenant mode is a configuration, not a migration. A team moves a workload onto a dedicated node, and back, with a labeling change, without rewriting anything and without leaving Titus. That turns the isolation decision into a reversible setting, which is the opposite of the one-way door between Titus and EC2 that teams used to face. A team can try single tenancy for a quarter, measure it, and step back if the trade-off isn’t worth it for them.What does not change is the contract. The Compute/Platform team still selects the instance type, patches the host, and sizes and scales the fleet underneath. The application team still uses the Titus API, the same delivery pipeline, and the same observability. Single tenancy is a new point on the isolation axis offered within the existing managed experience, not a separate product that the team has to learn and operate.When a dedicated node is the wrong callA dedicated node is a real cost, and single tenancy is not free isolation. Two things are worth weighing before reaching for it.First, a single-tenant task does not get the whole machine; it gets the machine minus overhead. Every Titus container host, dedicated or shared, runs the platform sidecars, system services, the kubelet, and the host environment itself, and that overhead is a roughly fixed slice of CPU and a few gigabytes of memory. On a shared host, that slice is paid once and amortized across the many tasks running there. On a dedicated node, a single task handles it. Because the cost is fixed rather than proportional, it is punishing as a fraction of a small instance and negligible on a large one: a small dedicated node can lose tens of percent of its resources to overhead, while on the largest shapes it rounds to a couple of percent.Second, because a task is placed on the smallest instance that fits it, there is usually a gap between what the task asked for and the next available shape, and on a dedicated node, that gap is pure waste, with no neighbors to soak it up. The two effects compound: fixed overhead plus the best-fit remainder set a ceiling on how much of a dedicated node a workload can actually use, and that ceiling is lowest exactly where people are tempted to reach for isolation casually, on small instances. However, this sizing waste can be reduced through coordination with the service owner as needed.The guidance follows from the arithmetic. Single tenancy pays off for large, long-running, performance-sensitive, disruption-sensitive workloads, sized close to a node shape and run as fewer, larger replicas rather than many small ones. It is the wrong call for small, bursty, or highly elastic workloads, where the overhead fraction is high, the dedicated node sits mostly idle, and multi-tenant packing is both cheaper and faster to scale. This is also why the mode is allowlisted rather than a self-serve checkbox: the platform can keep workloads on the side of that line where they belong, and leave the ones that would gain little from a node of their own on the shared fleet, where they are cheaper to run.Who’s using itThe first adopters are the workloads that motivated the work: real-time data infrastructure. Managed Apache Flink stream processing, streaming data connectors, and telemetry and logging pipelines were both the most frequent sources of network contention and the most damaged by it, because their recovery is expensive and their disruption budgets are tight. These are stateful, high-throughput jobs where a few seconds of starvation can cascade into minutes of catch-up, and where the platform’s own repacking used to be a source of disruption in its own right.Moving them onto dedicated nodes removed the class of problem rather than mitigating it. The teams running them report stable operation, having previously seen intermittent, hard-to-attribute interference, and their jobs are no longer relocated by fleet repacking, removing a second, self-inflicted source of disruption. Latency-sensitive serving paths and a handful of GraphQL and edge services have followed for the same reason: a predictable tail matters more to them than a few points of bin-packing efficiency.This is an ongoing rollout, not a finished one. We are widening the set of eligible workloads as we learn, using the largest production jobs as the stress test for the platform’s scaling assumptions, and watching the control-plane and EC2 launch-rate metrics as the count of small nodes grows. We have also been running periodic stress tests to exercise scaling ahead of real user workload, and making improvements to autoscaling and scheduling logic along the way.What’s nextWe are not done on either side of the tradeoff. On single tenancy, we are reducing launch latency with smarter pre-warming of common shapes, broadening the allowlist as scaling data holds up, and extending the model beyond long-running services as cost attribution and capacity stories mature. On the multi-tenant side, which remains the right default for most workloads, we are addressing the dimensions that hurt the most. The largest is the network: replacing HTB’s global-lock shaping with an eBPF-based Expected Departure Time approach that rate-limits by timestamping packets rather than contending on a lock, and pairing it with a lower-overhead container network device. We are also evaluating hardware cache and memory-bandwidth partitioning (Intel RDT and AMD PQoS) to give the kernel a real lever on the last-level cache, hardware GPU partitioning (NVIDIA MIG) for accelerator isolation, and continued work on the cgroup v2 IO controller for disk. This isolation benchmark lets us rank these by return on effort rather than by intuition, and show customers, in the numbers, that the shared fleet is getting quieter over time.Single-tenant Titus is also a step toward something larger. Netflix’s Platform teams offer two ways to get compute: virtual machines on EC2 & containers on Titus. We want to replace that with a single Compute API that takes intent rather than mechanism into account: how much isolation a workload needs, how quickly it must launch, how long it can run without disruption, and what business domain it belongs to. The platform then makes placement and runtime choices, and can make globally optimal ones because it sees the whole picture.ConclusionMulti-tenancy is the right default for a container platform, and we will keep making it better for everyone. But the right default is not right for everything. Single-tenant Titus gives the workloads that need it the isolation of a dedicated VM, provisioned and patched by our existing node management, under the same API and the same managed experience, without taking away the freedom to change their mind. We can now point to the difference rather than describe it: a tail that stops moving under a noisy neighbor, a fleet that packs more densely once spreading is retired, and hosts that are faster and safer to patch. For the streaming and data systems at the heart of Netflix’s real-time platform, a room of one’s own turned out to be the feature that mattered.Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Kubernetes] From Working Group to SIG Architecture: spotlight on AI Conformance
summary: In this SIG Architecture spotlight we talked with Janet Kuo (Google) and Yuan Tang (TensorScale AI) about the journey of AI Conformance in Kubernetes, from the initial Working Group to the integration SIG Architecture as a subproject. IntroductionsFrederico Muñoz and Kirti Goyal (FK): Hi Janet, Yuan, and thank you for the opportunity to learn a bit more about AI Conformance. Can you tell us a bit about yourselves and how you got involved in Kubernetes? Janet Kuo: I'm a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Google and have been a Kubernetes maintainer since 2015, joining the community just as we were racing toward the 1.0 launch. I started my journey writing the core workload controllers that standardized how applications are orchestrated on Kubernetes. Today, I lead SIG Apps as a Co-chair & TL, and also lead the AI Conformance program. My current focus is to ensure Kubernetes remains the best platform for the next generation of workloads, such as AI. Yuan Tang: I'm a co-founder of TensorScale AI where we build AI infrastructure for world models. Prior to that, I was a Senior Principal Software Engineer at Red Hat, where I led the development of Red Hat AI platform and upstream open source strategy. I became involved in Kubernetes early on by fostering collaborations between the Kubernetes community and projects I was leading, including Kubeflow, Argo, and KServe. I later helped found and lead WG Serving and the AI Conformance program, advancing innovation and strengthening community collaboration around running AI workloads on Kubernetes. Program, Working Group, Subproject: the many shapes of AI ConformanceFK: AI Conformance started as a CNCF Program, was it then you got involved? Janet Kuo: I was actually involved from day one since I pitched the original idea. It became obvious then that everyone was starting to run AI on Kubernetes, but vendors were building their infrastructure stacks in different ways. I got worried about ecosystem fragmentation. So I wrote up the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance Proposal, took it to the CNCF leadership to get their buy-in, and started the AI Conformance Program. Once we had the green light, I reached out to my fellow co-chairs Yuan Tang, Rita Zhang, and Mario Fahlandt to get the community rallied around it. Yuan Tang: Yes. I was a co-chair of WG Serving at that time and some of the initiatives such as the Gateway AI Inference Extension quickly gained traction. There was a strong interest among the community to include inference-related requirements in the Kubernetes AI Conformance program. FK: How would you describe the motivation behind the creation of the AI Conformance Working Group? Janet and Yuan: The motivation behind creating the Kubernetes AI Conformance Working Group (AI WG) was to address the rapid convergence of AI workloads onto Kubernetes while preventing ecosystem fragmentation. As AI adoption accelerated, organizations began running increasingly complex workloads, including distributed training, large-scale inference, GPU-intensive pipelines, and emerging agentic AI systems across many different Kubernetes platforms. However, vendors were implementing AI infrastructure capabilities differently, especially around GPUs, networking, scheduling, and inference orchestration. That created portability challenges, operational inconsistency, and growing vendor lock-in concerns. The AI WG was formed to bring the community together around: vendor-neutral AI infrastructure standards, interoperable Kubernetes-based AI platforms, consistent operational behavior for AI workloads, and common requirements for scalable AI deployment. FK: WGs are temporary by nature, based on outcomes: would you say the main goals of the WG were achieved? Janet and Yuan: Yes, the WG achieved its primary initial goals. The WG has succeeded in moving the ecosystem from: fragmented, vendor-specific AI infrastructure approaches to a shared, community-defined baseline for AI workloads on Kubernetes. Some concrete indicators of success include: Launching the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program Defining formal Kubernetes AI Requirements (KARs) Getting broad participation from major ecosystem players Growing certified platforms from 18 to 31 within a few months Aligning around newer Kubernetes primitives needed for AI workloads Establishing a roadmap for automated conformance verification Most importantly, the WG created consensus that AI workloads are now a first-class Kubernetes use case. FK: AI Conformance was specifically highlighted at the latest KubeCon: is this a reflection of the growing importance of AI throughout the project? Janet and Yuan: Yes, the prominence of AI Conformance at the latest KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is a strong reflection of how central AI has become to the Kubernetes ecosystem overall. A few years ago, AI workloads on Kubernetes were still viewed as somewhat specialized, mostly tied to ML platforms or GPU-heavy research environments. What’s changed is that AI is now becoming a mainstream infrastructure concern for nearly every large-scale platform operator. That shift naturally elevates AI from an application running on Kubernetes to a core workload category Kubernetes must optimize for. The AI Conformance initiative reflects that evolution. It signals that the community now sees AI infrastructure requirements, things like accelerator scheduling, high-performance networking, workload-aware orchestration, and low-latency inference, as important enough to standardize at the ecosystem level. Its visibility at KubeCon also shows a broader strategic realization: if Kubernetes is going to remain the universal control plane for modern infrastructure, it needs to provide a consistent foundation for AI workloads across clouds, on-prem, and edge environments. So the emphasis on AI Conformance is not just about chasing AI hype; it's about Kubernetes adapting to a major shift in workload patterns and ensuring the ecosystem evolves cohesively rather than fragmenting into vendor-specific AI stacks. From Working Group to SIG Architecture subprojectFK: How would you describe the change from WG to SIG? Is it a reflection of AI as something that requires ongoing architectural governance? Janet and Yuan: In Kubernetes, Working Groups are meant to be temporary. Our WG had a specific goal to get the initial Kubernetes AI Conformance requirements published and get the certification process off the ground. Once we hit those milestones, we archived the WG and moved AI Conformance to be a permanent subproject under SIG Architecture. Moving to SIG Architecture definitely proves that AI needs ongoing governance. AI isn’t just a passing trend or a one-off workload. It has become a core part of what Kubernetes runs every day. Because SIG Architecture already owns overall Kubernetes Conformance and API design principles, housing the AI Conformance subproject there makes perfect sense. It makes sure our AI Conformance requirements stay aligned with the rest of the Kubernetes ecosystem for the long haul. FK: And with that change, how would you describe the main goals and areas of intervention of the subproject? Janet and Yuan: Now that we’re a subproject, our main goal is to keep the AI Conformance standards current, vendor-neutral, and standard-setting. We want to make sure Kubernetes captures the latest advancements in AI infrastructure while keeping the ecosystem fair for everyone. When we find gaps where no clear community pattern exists, we help foster and form new standards to solve them. AI Conformance and KubernetesFK: AI Infrastructure is evolving very quickly, while Kubernetes APIs are designed to remain stable for years. Is this something you consider a challenge? Janet and Yuan: It’s definitely a tricky balance. AI moves very fast, while Kubernetes is designed to be stable and boring. But we actually structured the program around this exact tension. First, we use a tiered graduation model. When new AI infrastructure concepts emerge, we introduce them as recommended SHOULD requirements. That gives the ecosystem room to experiment and agree on best practices without locking Kubernetes into rigid APIs too early. Once those APIs stabilize and with ecosystem adoption, we graduate them to mandatory MUST requirements. Second, we intentionally keep our focus on the infrastructure layer. We test for core capabilities like accelerator support through Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA), rather than getting bogged down in specific AI frameworks or model servers. That keeps the base platform stable while letting the AI tooling evolve as fast as it needs to. FK: DRA has evolved, also due to the work of WG Device Management, as an important part of Kubernetes (and especially so for AI workloads), with SIG Architecture having an important role in how it’s integrated in Kubernetes: do you find any parallel in this? Specifically, do you think there will be a heavier focus in the integration with the evolving Kubernetes architecture as part of SIG Architecture? Janet and Yuan: There is a huge parallel there. Whenever we face a massive, complicated challenge that touches multiple parts of the codebase and involves multiple SIGs, a Working Group is the best place to start. It lets experts from different SIGs get together to figure out the problem, and build consensus. Being part of SIG Architecture means there will be a much heavier focus on how AI capabilities weave into the evolving Kubernetes architecture. Instead of treating AI as an add-on layer, we’re looking at how core Kubernetes primitives, like scheduling and resource allocation, need to adapt at a foundational level to support the next decade of AI workloads. Final remarksFK: For interested contributors, what’s the best way to get involved with the AI Conformance subproject? Janet and Yuan: We're always looking for new contributors. The easiest way to get started is by checking out our main repo at kubernetes-sigs/ai-conformance and join our meetings. If you're interested in defining new AI Conformance requirements, you can jump into PR reviews or propose your own using our KAR template. If you want to write code, we always need help expanding our automated Go test suites in the test/ directory. For vendors looking to certify their platforms, all the details are at cncf/k8s-ai-conformance. FK: Any final comments you would like to share? Janet and Yuan: We’ve been blown away by how fast the community has rallied around this. When we first announced the AI Conformance program during the keynote at KubeCon NA 2025, we weren’t sure what the response would be. But by the time we gave our update keynote at KubeCon EU 2026, we had grown from 18 certified platforms to 31 in just a few months. That kind of growth shows just how much the industry wanted a unified, vendor-neutral standard. It gives organizations the confidence that they can run their AI workloads on any certification Kubernetes platform without getting locked into a proprietary stack. If you’re a platform vendor, we’d love to see you get certified. If you’re a developer interested in the intersection of AI and cloud-native infrastructure, come join us in SIG Architecture! FK: Excellent, thank you both for guiding us in this journey on AI and AI Conformance in Kubernetes.

title: [CNCF] OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers
summary: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell, started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project, is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem: Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process: before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network: outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials: the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox, the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster. A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart. How a sandbox is created and run On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail. Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue (openshell/#1719) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator. Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018). OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back. OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. Which images run, how big a sandbox can get, which credentials it gets, and who can change OpenShell’s RBAC are left to the platform team. OpenShell vs. Agent Substrate Agent Substrate is another CNCF project that provides sandboxed execution for agents. Both projects applied, and were accepted, to the CNCF Sandbox in September, 2026 (#522 and #523). Both run each agent in its own sandbox on Kubernetes, but they are built differently. OpenShell uses the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project. Substrate has its own scheduler, controller, and sandbox runtime. Lin Sun’s CNCF post, Why sandboxing your agent is not enough, makes the case for Substrate: “Sandboxing your agents is necessary, but not sufficient.” Agent Sandbox is about running agents securely. Substrate is about running them securely and cheaply at scale, by suspending idle agents instead of giving each one a Pod. Agent Substrate is not meant to be used directly, but requires an orchestration layer like Agent Executor, Kagent, or possibly in the future OpenShell (more on that below). OpenShellAgent SubstrateOriginNVIDIAGoogleCNCF SandboxVoted in Sep 26, 2026Voted in Sep 28, 2026Main problemWhat may this agent do?How do we run thousands of mostly idle agents cheaply?Unit of workOne sandbox per agent: a Sandbox, a workload Pod, and a supervisor PodAn actor: an identity plus a snapshot. When active, it runs in its own sandbox inside a shared worker Pod. Workers are designed to hold many actors (–max-actors defaults to 1,000), but the autoscaling demo notes that each worker holds one actor todayKubernetes building blockAgent Sandbox. The gateway creates agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resources, and the Agent Sandbox controller reconciles themIts own WorkerPool CRD (ate.dev), which atecontroller turns into a Deployment of worker Pods. It does not use Agent SandboxRoutingThrough the gateway and the sandbox’s supervisorAn ate-target-actor header. The router resumes the actor if needed, and atunnel passes the request to its sandbox. Actors have no Pod IPCredentialsThe supervisor swaps a placeholder for the real key, only at endpoints the provider allowsThe egress gateway swaps an ate-secret:// placeholder header for the real credential. Actors and snapshots never hold the secretIdentitySupervisor identity tied to the namespace, Sandbox UID, Pod UID, and runtime generationA SPIFFE X.509 certificate per actor, valid for 1 hour, and mTLS between all components. OpenFGA access policies are in progressStateA /sandbox PVC that survives stop and startRAM and filesystem snapshots in object storage. Suspend and resume take under a second; the goal is 100 ms at p95AutoscalingHPA for the gateway (more than one replica needs external PostgreSQL) and node autoscalers. Sandbox has no /scale subresource, so HPA, KEDA, and VPA cannot target a sandbox. Each new agent is a gateway API callWorkerPool has a /scale subresource, so HPA can scale workers on how full they are (the demo runs on kind only), plus node autoscalers. Requests wait when the pool is fullMaturityv0.1.xPre-1.0. Three areas that will matter most to Kubernetes cluster admins:: How detailed the policy is. OpenShell checks each request at a supervisor that serves one sandbox. It can let curl read GitHub issues and block curl from creating one. Substrate checks traffic at a shared egress gateway, per actor and per destination host. There is work underway to natively support OpenFGA policies and allow external policy. What Kubernetes can see. Each OpenShell sandbox is a set of Kubernetes objects, so RBAC, Kyverno, audit logs, and kubectl work on it. Substrate keeps actors, templates, and egress policies in its own API, backed by PostgreSQL, so the Kubernetes API server is not on the request path. Admission control sees Substrate’s worker pools, but not the agents or their egress policies. Isolation. Substrate requires a gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor sandbox for every actor; a plain container is not supported. That is what makes its snapshots possible. OpenShell runs a standard container with Landlock and seccomp, and you can require a stronger RuntimeClass for untrusted agents. Scaling follows from this. With OpenShell, your application decides how many sandboxes to run, and you size each one when you create it, as the demo does with Kyverno defaults and caps. With Substrate, HPA scales the worker pools, and the number of agents is separate from the number of Pods. For now, choose based on your workload. If you have many bursty, mostly idle agents, such as one assistant per user, and cost per agent matters most, look at Substrate. If your agents hold real credentials and reach production systems, and you need per-request control and policy on Kubernetes objects, look at OpenShell. Many large enterprises will likely need a mix eventually, and in the future, you may be able to use both. OpenShell’s RFC 0012, merged Sep 10, 2026, makes isolation a pluggable isolation backend, separate from the supervisor that enforces policy. The team has proposed building a Substrate backend (NVIDIA/OpenShell#3362). OpenShell would keep the policy, credential, and audit controls, and Substrate would add gVisor isolation and suspend and resume that keeps memory. One blocker is fixed. #3366, merged Sep 21, means the shared contract no longer requires Landlock or seccomp evidence, so a gVisor backend can supply its own. Two pieces are still open: a versioned transport for a backend that runs in a separate process, and a lifecycle operation that keeps memory. As of Oct 11 the issue is open. A contributor has +1’d it and asked whether the maintainers would accept it, but no maintainer has replied yet. If it is accepted, you would get OpenShell’s per-request policy with Substrate’s density. Until then, the difference for admins is where policy runs. With OpenShell, Kyverno checks the sandboxes themselves. With Substrate, Kyverno checks the worker pools, and per-agent policy is set in Substrate’s own API. What Kyverno adds Kubernetes settings decide the sandbox Pod’s image, privileges, resources, credentials, and network rules. OpenShell checks some of these itself (step 6 above). RBAC and Kyverno, or other Kubernetes policy engines, help cover the rest. Start with RBAC. If only the gateway’s ServiceAccount and the Agent Sandbox controller can create Sandbox resources, other users cannot go around the gateway. Cluster-admins still can. RBAC decides who can use which verb on which resource type. It does not look at what a request contains, and it cannot add defaults. So these questions remain: Which images may agents run? How large can a sandbox get? Can an agent receive a raw API key? Can someone add wildcard permissions to an OpenShell Role, or open up the workload NetworkPolicy? Kyverno checks these at admission, for every user and ServiceAccount that sends requests to the sandbox namespace, including cluster-admins and the gateway. The demo’s kyverno-demo.sh runs six checks that RBAC cannot do. Then it creates a sandbox through OpenShell that passes all of them: ControlAttemptKyverno policyResultPod securityA Sandbox with a privileged: true containerenforce-sandbox-pod-securityDenied: “Every sandbox container must run as non-root, drop all capabilities, and disable privilege escalation.”RBACA Role named openshell-* that grants * verbs on * resourcesrestrict-openshell-rbacDenied: “OpenShell RBAC rules may not contain wildcards.”NetworkA patch that lets the openshell-sandbox-workloads NetworkPolicy allow all egressverify-openshell-network-boundaryDenied: “…may not allow direct workload egress.”Supply chainA Sandbox that uses the tag nicolaka/netshoot:v0.13enforce-sandbox-image-hygieneDenied: “Sandbox images must use immutable sha256 digest references.”ResourcesA Sandbox with no resources set, then one that asks for 8 CPU and 16Gi of memorydefault-sandbox-resources, enforce-sandbox-resource-boundsThe first gets defaults (100m CPU request). The second is denied: “at most 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, and 20Gi ephemeral storage”CredentialsA Sandbox that loads a Kubernetes Secret with envFromprotect-sandbox-credentialsDenied: “Use OpenShell providers instead of injecting Kubernetes Secrets…” A sandbox created through OpenShell with a digest-pinned image is admitted and keeps the 100m CPU request that Kyverno added. All seven policies run in Enforce mode. Six are ValidatingPolicy resources and one is a MutatingPolicy, all written in CEL. They match Sandbox resources, Roles and ClusterRoles named openshell-*, and the openshell-sandbox-workloads NetworkPolicy. The policies check the request, not the sender, so they also apply to the gateway. Even a compromised gateway cannot push a privileged, unpinned, or oversized Sandbox through admission. However, the gateway’s ServiceAccount can still create Pods and NetworkPolicies directly in the sandbox namespace. For production, extend the policies to Pods and to any NetworkPolicy that selects OpenShell workloads. The demo leaves out four more kinds of policy, because each needs signing keys or other setup first: Image verification: require Cosign signatures, SBOM and provenance attestations, and vulnerability checks for the gateway, supervisor, runtime, and agent images. Runtime class: require a RuntimeClass such as gVisor or Kata for untrusted agents. Workspace budgets: cap the number of sandboxes, their lifetime, and GPUs per workspace. Cleanup: delete idle sandboxes with Kyverno cleanup policies, and skip any under legal hold. Admission control only sees agents that OpenShell creates. A team’s own Deployment that calls api.openai.com never goes through the gateway or a supervisor. For that case, Nirmata’s Runtime for Kyverno, or other kernel monitors, run as a DaemonSet and attach eBPF programs to the Pods that a RuntimePolicy selects. It watches exec, file open, network, and DNS activity. In monitor mode it reports AI tools that nobody approved: agent CLIs such as claude or ollama, stdio MCP servers, *.gguf model files, and DNS lookups for model-provider hostnames. It writes findings as OpenReports in the Pod’s namespace. Future integrations can bring Kyverno policies to the OpenShell Supervisor for fine-grained control of sandbox operation allow and deny decisions. Closing thoughts Agents, and applications with LLM integrations, are becoming prominent workloads on Kubernetes. Admins will be asked to run them like everything else: isolated, audited, and under policy. OpenShell builds on Agent Sandbox instead of going around it, and it adds per-binary, per-request controls that Kubernetes objects cannot express. OpenShell checks the Pod settings it depends on and leaves the rest to you. This separation-of-concerns plays nicely with the CNCF ecosystem. The rest are Kubernetes objects, and admission control handles those well. Use RBAC to control who can create sandboxes. Use Kyverno to control what those sandboxes may contain, and other Kubernetes configurations, starting with the seven policies in the demo. OpenShell controls the agent, and Kyverno controls the rest. To try it yourself: git clone https://github.com/nirmata/demo-openshell cd demo-openshell ./scripts/setup.sh && ./scripts/install-cli.sh && ./scripts/verify.sh ./scripts/demo.sh # OpenShell L7 policy ./scripts/kyverno-demo.sh # Kyverno admission policies ./scripts/cleanup.sh You need Docker, kind, kubectl, Helm, curl, SSH, and nc. Then try the policies on your own OpenShell cluster and tell us what breaks.
