title: [Slack Engineering] Slack AI: The Path to Multi-Cloud
summary: In early 2023, Slack faced a foundational challenge: serving Large Language Models (LLMs) at enterprise scale with the security, reliability, and performance our customers expect. Over three years, we evolved from basic infrastructure to orchestrating a sophisticated multi-cloud architecture. We didn’t just want shiny new models; we needed a system resilient to regional outages and GPU scarcity. Our journey moved through four distinct phases, shifting from reactive infrastructure management to proactive, multi-vendor orchestration. Phase 1: The SageMaker Era When we built the initial stages of Slack AI, AWS SageMaker was the natural starting point. It was a managed ML Serving platform that offered the key things that we were looking for: Security, FedRamp compliance, model availability and control. We were able to leverage a sophisticated escrow virtual private cloud (VPC) strategy to establish a strict zero-knowledge environment: our data remained private to Slack, and the provider’s proprietary model weights remained inaccessible to us. To maximize uptime for a global user base, we deployed these containers across multiple AWS regions. This required our teams to manage the operational lifecycle, including cross-region IAM roles, balanced routing across model endpoints, proactive capacity planning, and auto-scaling logic. The Operational Reality While SageMaker provided the necessary security, the overhead was immense. We faced three primary taxes: Scaling Latency: Initialization times prevented instantaneous scaling. Hardware Scarcity: Enterprise-grade Nvidia GPUs, such as the A100 (Ampere architecture) and the emerging H100 (Hopper architecture) instances, were often unavailable. Over-Provisioning: Maintaining idle resources to meet peak SLAs. By early 2024, we mitigated these via On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCR) and proactive, cron-based scaling. However, this reinforced a hard truth: we were spending too many engineering cycles on plumbing. To scale, we needed automated capacity, not manual coordination. Feature Lag As the AI ecosystem and feature usage accelerated, newer and higher quality models emerged quickly. While we were maintaining a custom serving solution on SageMaker, AWS was heavily prioritizing Amazon Bedrock, its purpose-built managed LLM service. Hosting Anthropic models via an escrow VPC led to a “catch-up” cycle. Model iterations and optimizations often debuted on Bedrock weeks or months before SageMaker availability. For Slack, where staying at the bleeding edge of model quality is a competitive necessity, this gap became a significant driver for our next architectural evolution. Phase 2: Migrating to Amazon Bedrock for Agility and Access By mid-2024, AWS Bedrock had matured significantly. It had achieved FedRamp Moderate compliance and also promised the same security posture that we required. The decision to migrate was a strategic pivot as it offered three immediate advantages: Operational Simplicity: We moved away from having to scale individual GPU instances to a fully managed AWS service. Immediate Model Access: We eliminated any LLM model feature lag by gaining access to the latest models very quickly after LLM Providers made them publicly available. Infrastructure Efficiency: Bedrock introduced Provisioned Throughput (PT) and On Demand (OD) infrastructure options, allowing us to tailor compute to specific use cases. We utilized PT for interactive, latency-sensitive features like channel summaries, while leveraging OD for bursty, scheduled workloads like Recap to eliminate costs for idle compute. Understanding Provisioned Throughput In the Bedrock ecosystem, capacity is measured in Model Units (MUs). Each MU provides a deterministic amount of throughput, measured in tokens per minute. Shifting from GPU instances to MUs allowed us to abstract away the hardware and focus entirely on raw throughput. To minimize migration risk, we prioritized provisioned throughput infrastructure first, leaving on demand infra as a fast follow. The Zero Incident Migration We executed the transition through a multi-stage migration strategy: Compliance: Secured Legal, Security, and FedRamp sign-offs before rerouting production traffic to maintain our existing high bar for data privacy. Capacity: Conducted extensive load tests to map the exact number of Model Units (MUs) required to match our SageMaker baseline across diverse traffic profiles. Quality: Used A/B testing and evaluation frameworks to compare environment outputs side-by-side, verifying both quality and latency parity. Rollout: Implemented gradual traffic shifts via feature flags and instant rollback capabilities, ensuring 100% availability during the switch. Achieving Operational Maturity The migration to Bedrock delivered immediate, compounding wins for our engineering teams and our customers: Engineering Efficiency & Enhanced Experience: By offloading the burden of self-managed infrastructure, we freed our engineers to focus on model performance and feature quality. Because Bedrock serves as the primary launchpad for new LLMs, we were able to deliver model upgrades and quality improvements to users weeks or months earlier than was possible on SageMaker, directly enhancing the user experience across the entire Slack AI suite. A prime example was our ability to quickly upgrade the AI Search features to new high-reasoning models, which led to more precise, context-aware answers. Architectural Simplicity: We successfully moved away from the “infrastructure plumbing” of endpoint management, GPU instance lifecycle, and complex capacity reservation coordination. In this new model, we simply requested quota from AWS, they provisioned the MUs, and we served traffic. This allowed us to shift from reactive scaling to a strategic forecasting technique. By projecting our needs several weeks out, we gave our account teams ample time to secure capacity, ensuring we were always ahead of the demand curve. The “Zero-Incident” Standard: Switching an entire backend while serving live traffic can sometimes be a recipe for disaster. We avoided that by being borderline obsessed with parity, and achieved zero customer-facing incidents. We didn’t just run unit tests; we ran massive load tests and shadow requests to find the exact “Model Unit” count that matched our old setup. We used feature flags to slowly bleed traffic over, so if anything looked even slightly off, we could yank it back in seconds. It wasn’t magic – it was just a lot of cautious plumbing. This solidified a core Slack AI engineering principle: measure first, migrate gradually, and monitor continuously. The Final Efficiency Gap While Provisioned Throughput was a massive leap forward for predictable, consistent workloads, it wasn’t perfectly optimized for the workloads. We encountered two primary efficiency hurdles: The Over-Provisioning Cycle: Our infrastructure needs are very closely aligned by the global workday traffic patterns. To ensure a snappy experience during the massive US East and West Coast morning surges – when users lean heavily on AI Summaries and Search to catch up on activity – we had to maintain a high baseline of MUs. While we saw steadier, lighter usage during the APAC and EU mornings, we had to provision for that absolute global peak. This meant we were often paying for significant underutilized capacity during the troughs between regional handoffs and over the weekends, creating a persistent efficiency gap. The Commitment Lock-in: Provisioned Throughput often required commitments of one to six months. In the fast-moving world of LLMs, where a state-of-the-art model can be superseded in weeks, these commitments effectively slowed down our ability to upgrade. Even when a superior model was released, we often chose to wait for our existing commitments to expire before migrating. These challenges led us to our next evolution: finding a way to balance the reliability of provisioned capacity with the economic and technical flexibility of On-Demand scaling. Phase 3: Transitioning to Bedrock On-Demand With high confidence in Bedrock and mature monitoring, we moved to close the final efficiency and quality gap. Historical analysis revealed that feature usage fluctuated with business hours, leaving some idle capacity overnight. Rather than maintaining a static footprint for 24/7 peak capacity, moving to on-demand infrastructure allowed us to solve the idle capacity problem. It gave us the architectural agility to support highly variable workloads without the friction of manual over-provisioning. For features with a 10x variance between peak and off-peak hours, the efficiency gains were substantial. More importantly, it removed the technical bottleneck we faced in Phase 2: because we were no longer locked into multi-month commitments, we regained the freedom to migrate features to different models. This meant that as soon as a more performant model dropped and passed our internal quality and metrics bars, we could pivot our infrastructure to support it within a day, rather than waiting months for a contract to expire. The Hybrid Strategy: Optimizing for Performance and Fluency We didn’t simply flip a switch and move everything to On-Demand. To balance efficiency with a premium user experience, we implemented a Hybrid Routing strategy. We kept high-volume, latency-sensitive features on dedicated capacity (Provisioned Throughput) to ensure a consistent “snappy” feel. Simultaneously, we moved asynchronous, bursty workloads – like nightly Recaps – to On-Demand capacity. To bridge the gap, we engineered a Spillover Pattern: if a sudden surge pushed us beyond our reserved limits, excess requests automatically “spilled over” to on-demand endpoints, ensuring we never dropped a request due to capacity ceilings. Navigating the Trade-offs of On-Demand Shifting to On-Demand traded rigid pre-planning for architectural agility, eliminating manual capacity management. By utilizing Bedrock’s ability to route across different US regions based on real-time availability, we were able to find capacity dynamically while adhering to our regional data boundaries. However, this flexibility introduced a new set of variables that we had to solve for: Service Level Variability: Unlike the dedicated nature of PT, OD operates on a shared-resource model, which typically carries different uptime characteristics. Regional Capacity Orchestration: Success with OD relies on the cloud provider’s ability to manage demand across their entire customer base in specific regions, rather than having specific hardware units explicitly reserved for Slack. Concentration Risk: Relying too heavily on a single provider’s on-demand pool meant that any service-wide blip could have the potential to impact entire Slack AI features simultaneously. Engineering for Resilience To mitigate these risks, we didn’t just accept the trade-offs – we built a more intelligent AI Platform abstraction. We developed a model hierarchy for every AI feature, allowing our system to automatically fall back to different models if the primary model reached a degraded state. Some examples of regressions are elevated time to first token latencies, throttling errors, and downward trend in customer feedback. This hierarchy was a game-changer for model quality and reliability. If a specific model was underperforming or hitting limits in one region, the platform would reroute the request in real-time to another healthy endpoint. From the customer’s perspective, the experience remained seamless; they continued to receive high-quality results without ever knowing a complex failover had occurred behind the scenes. While this internal fallback logic significantly increased our service resilience, it also highlighted two strategic gaps. First, no matter how many failovers we engineered within a single cloud, we remained susceptible to any potential provider-wide outage. Second, the AI landscape is moving with incredible velocity and remains highly fragmented. The state-of-the-art model for a specific task – whether it’s summarization, reasoning, or high-speed extraction – can change in a matter of weeks, and these leading models are often exclusive to specific cloud providers. Relying on any single vendor meant we might be artificially limiting our access to the highest-quality technology available. To ensure Slack AI always provides the best possible experience, we need the flexibility to go wherever the best models are while simultaneously meeting our security, compliance, and privacy standards. As Slack AI scaled to millions of users, we realized that true enterprise-grade reliability and a “best-of-breed” model strategy required looking beyond any single provider. This realization was the primary catalyst for our latest evolution: the move to a Multi-Cloud architecture. Phase 4: Expanding to a Multi-Cloud Strategy Ecosystem We recognized that providing a world-class AI experience required the best of every ecosystem. By early-2026 we officially expanded our footprint to include Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Vertex AI, not just as a failover for redundancy, but as a strategic engine to accelerate product innovation through access to a broader catalog of state-of-the-art models. Our goal is simple: ensure Slack remains the most intelligent place to get work done. This move wasn’t done just for the sake of complexity, but rather a strategic shift driven by four key factors: Infrastructural Redundancy & High Availability: For a mission-critical Digital HQ, uptime is the primary metric. While we continue to rely on third-party LLM models as a cornerstone for their consistency and reliability, a multi-cloud footprint eliminates provider-level large scale infrastructural disruptions as a single point of failure. If an entire cloud ecosystem experiences a regional or platform-wide disruption, our traffic can be rerouted to a separate, healthy stack without service interruption. Model-to-Feature Optimization: The “one-size-fits-all” approach to LLMs quickly hits diminishing returns. By expanding our catalog to include multiple models, we gained the ability to match the specific latent strengths of a model to the specific requirements of a feature. This granular optimization led to immediate performance gains: ~10% improvement in quality metrics for complex reasoning tasks. ~67% reduction in latency for high-velocity, low-token workloads. Access to Innovation: The AI landscape moves at extreme velocity with frequent vendor exclusivity. Multi-cloud ensures we are ready to integrate with the latest breakthroughs regardless of where they are hosted while upholding our compliance, privacy, and security promises. Dynamic Workload Orchestration: Beyond simple failover, multiple providers allow for sophisticated traffic shaping. We can route requests based on real-time telemetry – evaluating not just provider health, but which endpoint offers the optimal performance profile for a given workload at that exact moment. This enhanced our infrastructure from a static resource into a dynamic, intelligent routing layer. The Integration Journey Building a production-ready GCP integration was a massive cross-functional effort. It required tight synchronization across teams such as Security, Risk and Compliance, Trust and Integrity, AI Quality, Legal, and Cloud Providers to ensure our data boundaries remained ironclad across the board. Expanding to GCP Vertex AI turned our infrastructure into a strategic engine for product innovation. Rather than being limited to any single provider’s catalog, we can now granularly match specific features to the models best suited for them – balancing factors like context window, latency, and reasoning capabilities. To make this a reality, we solved cold start engineering hurdles by implementing secretless authentication and an API Normalization layer that translates disparate provider signals into a unified language for our application logic. Architectural Deep Dive: The Intelligent Routing Layer The core technical challenge was building a system that abstracted away provider complexity. By enhancing our abstraction layer into an Intelligent Routing Layer, we ensured that users receive the fastest, highest-quality response available. If one model or provider slows down, the system instantly reroutes the request to a better-performing alternative, making the underlying complexity completely invisible to the user while maintaining a seamless experience. It contains: Metric-Driven Model Selection: We use our internal quality metrics to determine the optimal model for each feature. For instance, if our benchmarks show a specific LLM outperforms others for “Recaps,” the router directs traffic accordingly. Crucially, we always designate backup models for every feature; if the primary choice doesn’t meet our performance or quality thresholds in real-time, the system knows exactly where to go next. Experimental Rules & A/B Testing: This capability has fundamentally changed our release velocity. When we wanted to test the latest LLMs, after our security and compliance verifications, for our Recaps feature, we were able to route a percentage of traffic to the new model with minimal code changes and an incredibly fast turnaround time. This allowed us to validate performance in the wild and tighten our feedback loop from weeks to days. Automated Circuit Breaker & Health Monitoring: To move beyond manual failovers, we implemented an automated Circuit Breaker pattern. This system acts as a real-time watchdog, constantly monitoring health signals at the endpoint level. If a specific provider or model begins to exhibit signs of distress – such as an elevated Time to First Token (TTFT), a spike in 5xx error rates, or crossing a latency p90 threshold – the circuit “trips.” Once tripped, the routing layer automatically diverts traffic to a healthy alternative model based on the use case and complexity. Crucially, the breaker enters a partial-open state, allowing a small, controlled trickle of requests to reach the degraded endpoint. As the endpoint demonstrates sustained health, the system dynamically expands this trickle, incrementally ramping traffic back up until the breaker is fully “closed” and normal operations resume. This ensures a graceful recovery without overwhelming a stabilizing service. The Multi-Cloud Reality Running a multi-cloud footprint at our scale is a major technical undertaking. It’s a conscious trade-off: we gain immense flexibility but it requires a much more sophisticated approach to how we manage our systems: API and Behavioral Friction: Each provider has its own unique API patterns, proprietary error codes, and distinct rate-limiting behaviors. We had to build a robust normalization layer to ensure that a “Rate Limit Exceeded” from one provider and a “Throttling Exception” from another were handled identically by our application logic. Operational Monitoring Complexity: To avoid blind spots, we couldn’t rely on the native dashboards of each cloud. We had to build a unified monitoring stack that integrates telemetry from the multiple clouds into a single view, ensuring our on-call engineers can diagnose issues without pivoting between consoles. The Attribution Challenge: Accurately tracking the cost per feature internally becomes significantly harder when workloads are shifting dynamically between clouds. This required deep instrumentation across multiple billing systems to maintain financial transparency. The On-Call Knowledge Gap: Our engineers can no longer be specialists in just one ecosystem. To support the platform effectively, they need to be provider agnostic, possessing deep expertise in the infrastructure patterns and networking nuances that span multiple major cloud environments. This shift requires a broader skill set to troubleshoot and maintain a distributed, multi-vendor footprint. While multi-cloud increases operational overhead, the trade-off is a superior service. We have removed single points of failure, improved quality benchmarks by matching features to specific model strengths, and gained the strategic leverage to adopt new innovations the moment they hit the market. Reflections on the Path to Multi-Cloud We arrived at a multi-cloud architecture not for the sake of complexity, but to enhance Slack’s standards for product innovation and reliability. Looking back, five themes stand out: 1. Scaling safely requires XFN parity The biggest hurdles in scaling AI aren’t just technical; they also include legal, risk, compliance, and security related tasks. Achieving deep alignment between these teams and engineering is what allowed us to scale to millions of users without compromising our trust standards. 2. The abstraction layer is a core requirement As seen in our Phase 2 move, the most critical decision wasn’t which model to use, but how we built the logic around them. Agility and speed to market are our primary competitive edge. 3. Treat architecture as a living document Managed services mature monthly. Because we remained provider-agnostic, we can now adopt breakthroughs in latency or reasoning without a total rewrite. 4. Reliability requires provider agnosticism Internal failovers aren’t enough. Our move in Phase 4 to a multi-provider stack ensures Slack stays online even during any potential platform-wide cloud disruption. 5. Redefining the meaning of “Failure” An LLM service that is “up” but slow is effectively broken. By treating different dimensions of data such as p90 spikes as soft failures and feedback trends, our routing layer ensures users have a snappy experience. The future of enterprise AI is multi-cloud, multi-model, and dynamically orchestrated. By prioritizing portability and staying close to the market, we haven’t just built a way to use AI – we’ve built a platform that harnesses the best the industry has to offer the moment it arrives. We’re looking forward to seeing what we build next! Interested in taking on interesting projects, making people’s work lives easier, or just building some pretty cool forms? We’re hiring! Apply now

title: [Netflix] Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
summary: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-SilvaWhen Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.This post is about that search for the needle.The Four hours before a fixConsider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.The MELT Layer“What caused the issue?”Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system.The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves outThe timeline of an investigationSo how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hoursIn our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.The disagreement underneathThe instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.The OntologyThis agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.api-gateway rdf:type ops:Application .api-gateway ops:ownedBy "Team Bedrock" .api-gateway ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .INC-5377 rdf:type ops:Incident .INC-5377 ops:affects api-gateway .INC-5377 ops:severity "SEV 2" .In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:Creating determinism from non-determinismBuilding this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:category IN sentiment IN # Result — a deterministic triple:thread:123 slack:category "incident" .thread:123 slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:The five layers to create determinism from non-determinismEnrichers: Agents as entropy reducersWe use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:class Enricher: async def _enrich_async(self, ...): raw = await self.fetch(...) # 1. read noisy input result = self.analyze(raw) # 2. process (may be stochastic) graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X)) # 3. emit TYPED triples graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value))) return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:every entity carries an rdf:type,every URI follows a single naming scheme, andthe catalog gates every ops:Application.Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chainsThe correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.The Correlation EngineThe role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.The knowledge flywheelEach harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.The Knowledge FlywheelObserve collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.Putting the graph to workOn top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.If you want to build one of theseA fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.What comes nextThe graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.AcknowledgementsNone of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Designing for sovereign AI: A shared foundation from edge to cloud
summary: As organizations apply AI to more business-critical and data-intensive workloads, AI processing is moving closer to where data is created, decisions are made, and operations take place. Manufacturers can analyze confidential production data next to the systems that generate it. Pharmaceutical companies can apply AI to clinical trials within controlled environments. Government agencies can run AI applications on sensitive information while maintaining established security and operational boundaries. This shift reflects ongoing innovation across the technology ecosystem to give organizations greater flexibility in where they run AI and process sensitive data, and it is changing the digital sovereignty conversation. It now encompasses where data is stored and processed, where workloads run, who can access and operate the systems around them, and how those systems remain secure and operational as requirements change. The next phase of digital sovereignty will take shape across the technology ecosystem, through closer alignment among silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI. Learn more about digital sovereignty As AI extends into more sensitive and mission-critical workloads, sovereignty must be designed across the stack, from silicon and infrastructure to cloud, data, and AI. Microsoft and Intel® are working together to help organizations create a more consistent foundation for innovation, while retaining greater choice over where workloads run and how they are controlled. A flexible sovereign architecture allows organizations to place each workload in the right environment, apply the controls it requires, and maintain a more consistent technology and operating foundation as requirements evolve. Sovereignty must work across the technology stack Sovereignty requirements vary by workload. The right level of control depends on factors such as data sensitivity, regulation, latency, connectivity, operational access, and resilience requirements. This creates a continuum, where organizations can apply different levels of control across public cloud, customer-controlled environments, and trusted partner solutions. Delivering that flexibility requires the underlying technology layers to work together. The controls that shape where a workload runs, how data is protected, who can access it, and how the environment is verified extend across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI. This is where the Microsoft and Intel partnership comes into focus. Together, we are working to create a more consistent foundation across these layers, giving organizations greater choice in where workloads run and how they are controlled. This principle is central to the work between Microsoft and Intel. Azure Local, running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors, brings distributed Azure infrastructure together with a common compute foundation for customer-controlled environments. Organizations can extend cloud and AI capabilities closer to their data and operations while maintaining consistent approaches to security, management, and governance. Trust must be designed for and verified For sensitive workloads, trust must be supported by technical protections and verifiable evidence. Organizations need to protect workloads across the technology stack and verify that systems are operating under the security conditions they have established. That starts at the compute layer and extends through identity, encryption, governance, policy, and operations. For supported Azure Confidential VM configurations, Intel® Xeon® processors provide hardware-based protections, including Intel® Trust Domain Extensions (Intel TDX), which can help isolate workloads while they are in use. Hardware-backed attestation can provide evidence that helps organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. Microsoft extends this foundation through security and governance controls across cloud and customer-controlled environments. Together, these capabilities can help organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. This is particularly important as AI brings regulated, proprietary, and mission-critical data into new workloads. Each workload should receive protections proportionate to its risk. Isolation, encryption, attestation, and operational controls can be applied where they provide meaningful value while preserving a manageable operating model across the broader environment. Digital sovereignty requires trust across the technology stack. Together, Intel and Microsoft are combining hardware-based security and confidential computing with cloud, AI and distributed infrastructure to help customers protect sensitive workloads and verify the environments in which they run. This shared foundation gives organizations greater control, confidence and choice, with the performance and scale to continue innovating as AI moves into more regulated and mission-critical environments. —Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security Sovereign AI brings intelligence closer to data Much of the data with the greatest potential for AI must remain within defined operational, regulatory, or security boundaries. This includes data tied to industrial operations, government services, clinical environments, intellectual property, and proprietary research. Workload placement has therefore become a practical AI decision. Organizations need the flexibility to run AI closer to their data, applications, and operations. Delivering that flexibility requires infrastructure, cloud platforms, AI software, and security capabilities to work as a connected foundation. Microsoft Foundry helps organizations build and deploy AI applications and models, with options for where AI runs based on their requirements. Foundry Local enables organizations to run AI inference in their own environments, closer to the data and applications those models rely on. On the same infrastructure, Intel Xeon 6 processors with Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX) can accelerate AI workloads directly on the CPU. Intel® OpenVINO™ helps developers optimize and deploy models across supported infrastructure. This approach extends across the broader application environment. Organizations may need to manage AI, applications, data, development, and productivity workloads within the same governance and operational boundary. Microsoft 365 Local and GitHub Enterprise Local extend customer-controlled options to collaboration, source code, and software development workflows. Sovereign AI brings models, data, applications, development tools, and infrastructure together under the controls each workload requires. This approach allows organizations to apply AI within the operational and governance boundaries established for their most sensitive data. Organizations want to apply AI to their most valuable data while maintaining the controls that data requires. On supported Azure confidential VM configurations, Intel TDX helps make that possible by running AI workloads in hardware-isolated trust domains, protecting models and data while in use and isolating them from the host and hypervisor. Hardware-backed attestation then gives organizations evidence they can check against their own requirements, so they can move from trusting their environment to verifying it. —Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security Sovereignty architecture must be adaptable Sovereignty requirements will continue to change. A workload that runs in a connected environment today may face different regulatory, resilience, or connectivity requirements tomorrow. AI models, applications, and infrastructure will also continue to evolve. A sovereign architecture must therefore provide control without creating rigidity. Organizations should be able to adapt where workloads run, how they are secured, and how they connect without rebuilding their management and security model each time requirements change. This is another reason partnership across the technology stack matters. Alignment across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI software can give organizations a more stable foundation even as individual technologies and workload requirements evolve. A well-designed sovereign architecture gives organizations room to respond as regulations, technologies, and operating conditions change. Explore Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe Discover how Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe helps organizations address evolving data sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements while accelerating cloud and AI innovation. Learn more Three questions leaders should ask Digital sovereignty can become abstract quickly. A better place to start is the workload. 1. What must remain under your control? Consider the data, infrastructure, administrative access, software operations, and connectivity on which the workload depends. The answer may differ by application, even within the same organization. 2. Can you verify that those controls are working? Policies and contractual commitments are important, but sensitive workloads may also require technical evidence. Consider how your architecture supports encryption, isolation, identity and access control, policy enforcement, attestation, and operational transparency. 3. Will the architecture leave you room to adapt? AI capabilities, regulations, operating conditions, and workload requirements will continue to change. Your architecture should allow you to adopt new models, move processing closer to data, and adjust where workloads run without creating an entirely separate technology environment each time. Digital sovereignty depends on cloud, infrastructure, security, AI, and silicon working together. Our collaboration with Intel gives customers a more consistent foundation across these layers, so they can apply stronger controls where needed while retaining the flexibility to innovate. —Bernardo Caldas, CVP, Azure Edge Product Management The strongest sovereignty strategy preserves choice Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control over the technology and data they depend on while preserving their capacity to innovate. Achieving that outcome requires collaboration across the technology ecosystem. Microsoft and Intel are connecting silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI to give organizations greater flexibility in where workloads run, how they are protected, and how they evolve. A shared foundation across these layers allows organizations to apply the right controls to each workload and benefit from advances across the broader technology ecosystem. A strong sovereignty strategy meets today’s requirements while preserving tomorrow’s options. Resources to learn more Dive deeper into digital sovereignty to learn how Microsoft is helping organizations address data residency, operational control, security, and regulatory requirements across cloud and customer-controlled environments. Learn more about Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud. Join us at Microsoft Ignite in November to hear the latest on Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, Azure Local, AI, security, and infrastructure innovation. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available
summary: Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define. Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes. Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems. Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path. For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in action To show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide. The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context. I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues. The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict. The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from. The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow. The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from. The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context. In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships. Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page. To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts. — Esra
