title: [HashiCorp] Announcing the public preview of HashiCorp Vault Arc: Evolve security for emerging workloads
summary: Enterprises rely on HashiCorp Vault to secure access to sensitive systems, applications, and data across increasingly complex hybrid and multi-cloud environments. But the environment around those applications is changing. Machine identities continue to grow, certificate lifecycles are becoming shorter, cryptographic requirements are evolving, and AI agents are creating a new class of autonomous workload that must be identified, authorized, and governed. Today, we are announcing the public preview of Vault Arc, expanding the Vault portfolio with new capabilities designed for these emerging security and operational requirements. Vault Arc is still Vault. It builds on the role Vault plays in enterprise security while introducing a new approach to how security resources are modeled, governed, queried, and operated. Importantly, Vault Arc complements Vault Enterprise rather than requiring customers to replace it. Organizations can continue deploying and expanding Vault Enterprise for existing and new workloads while evaluating Vault Arc where its capabilities provide additional value. Extending Vault for what's next Modernization isn't simply about replacing existing technology. It's about giving organizations the flexibility to respond as their infrastructure, workloads, and security requirements change. Vault Arc introduces a resource-based approach to Security Lifecycle Management. Security resources can be represented with unique resource identities designed to make them easier to understand, query, govern, and incorporate into security policy. This approach provides a foundation for several important capabilities: More intuitive authorization and governance. Vault Arc separates access grants from broader governance policies, helping organizations establish enterprise guardrails while allowing teams to manage appropriate access within those boundaries. Greater visibility and auditability. Typed, queryable resources make it easier for security and platform teams to understand what exists in their environment and answer questions about credentials and other security resources. Simplified operations and developer workflows. Vault Arc is designed to reduce operational complexity while making common workflows easier to consume through APIs, automation, and streamlined user experiences. Cryptographic agility. As cryptographic standards evolve, Vault Arc provides a foundation for more policy-driven approaches to managing keys, certificates, algorithms, and future cryptographic transitions. Preparing for machine and agentic workloads The growth of non-human identities is changing what enterprises need from identity and secrets management. AI agents accelerate that change. Agents can perform different tasks, interact with multiple tools and systems, and take actions on behalf of people and applications. The authority an agent requires can therefore depend on its identity, current task, context, and mandate. Treating these agents simply as another long-lived service account risks losing that context. Vault Arc is being designed with these emerging workloads in mind. The public preview establishes capabilities for agent identity governance, scoped and ephemeral authorization, and auditable agent activity. Organizations can begin moving toward a model in which agent access is tied more closely to identity, policy, and the work being performed. This represents an important step toward Agentic Security Lifecycle Management (SLM), where organizations can govern what an agent represents, what it is authorized to do, what credentials and resources it can access, and what actions it performs throughout its lifecycle. Modernization without a forced migration Vault Enterprise and Vault Arc are designed to coexist, giving organizations the flexibility to determine where each best meets their requirements. Customers can continue deploying Vault Enterprise while evaluating and adopting Vault Arc incrementally based on individual applications, workloads, and use cases. This approach allows modernization to happen at the pace of the enterprise rather than according to an arbitrary migration deadline. Organizations can progressively evaluate and introduce new capabilities while reducing the disruption and risk traditionally associated with major platform transitions. Extending governance across Vault As organizations expand their Vault footprint, they also need greater visibility and governance across an increasingly distributed security estate. Secure Hub, also entering public preview, complements this strategy by providing centralized visibility, reporting, and governance across Vault environments, including Vault Enterprise and Vault Arc. This gives organizations greater enterprise-wide context while controls and enforcement remain within individual Vault environments. Together, Vault Arc and Secure Hub provide organizations with greater flexibility to introduce new capabilities while developing a more consistent governance model across their broader Vault estate. Expanding security lifecycle management Together with Vault Enterprise, Secure Hub, and capabilities across the broader IBM security portfolio, Vault Arc advances a Security Lifecycle Management strategy designed for environments in which humans, applications, machines, and increasingly autonomous agents all require secure access to enterprise resources. The public preview gives customers an opportunity to experience that direction firsthand and provide feedback that helps shape the evolution of Vault Arc. Join the HashiCorp Vault Arc public preview to explore the new capabilities, share your feedback, and evaluate how Secure Hub can extend your organization's Security Lifecycle Management strategy. Learn more about the SLM announcements at TechXchange.

title: [Cloudflare] See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
summary: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site.Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business.See how agents access your siteKnowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time.In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use.For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. The population overview page shows which personal agents are active across your users and how many accounts use them, so you can determine whether agent traffic is a meaningful part of your business. Every login and sign-up event now shows whether a personal agent made the request, and which one. Fraud teams can filter accounts by AI assistant events or number of AI assistants.Additionally, each user's account overview shows the agents acting for that account. A fraud analyst investigating an unusual login can tell whether it came from an agent the customer has relied on for weeks, or from an agent that appeared for the first time today and needs a closer look. If it looks like an attacker is using an agent on an account, fraud analysts can mitigate that account directly, with a WAF rule on its Hashed User ID, without blocking the agent for everyone else who relies on it.Together, these views give you a clearer basis for deciding which personal agents to welcome, limit, or block.Set access policies that reflect your preferencesWe introduced AI bot policies this summer so site owners could make separate access control choices for AI bots used for Search, Training, and Agent behaviors. Now we’re expanding the existing Agents policy to include granular control options for supported personal agents. To reflect this broader scope, we’re renaming the setting AI Crawler and Agent access policies.In Security Settings, you can set an overall Agents policy, then choose a different policy for each supported personal agent: Allow (do not block), Block on pages with ads, or Block. For example, you can set the overall Agents policy to Block on pages with ads, then choose Allow (do not block) for a supported personal agent you want to welcome. Your existing Search and Training policies stay as they are.You can also make these choices when you add a new zone to Cloudflare. During onboarding, we ask whether you monetize pages with ads and then tailor the recommended policies to your answer. You can always revisit your access controls later in Security Settings.The right policy depends on your site. One publisher may allow a supported personal agent throughout its site so readers can find its articles, while another may block that same agent on pages where ads support the content. Both publishers are choosing the access control that works for their business.Agent identity is only part of the storyThe analytics and policies we’re launching today give site owners visibility into personal agent activity and control over their access. Our next goal is to help site owners preserve the context of their relationships with users when personal agents act as intermediaries. A site may recognize the agent making a request but lack information it would otherwise have about the user: whether they are an existing customer, what they authorized the agent to do, whether they have a subscription, or which protections should apply.Reaching that goal will require privacy-aware ways to (1) carry user context through an agent, (2) help sites assess reputation, and (3) establish clear accountability when something goes wrong. We’ll be sharing more as we work with agent operators and others across the ecosystem, so site owners can choose whether to grant agents greater access while continuing to build relationships with their users. Make the choice for your siteThat person asking a personal agent to compare products, find support, or complete a purchase is still a customer trying to reach your business. Review how personal agents are accessing your site, then visit Security Settings → AI Crawler and Agent access policies to set the terms that work for your site.

title: [Dropbox Tech] Evolving our calendar assistant Reclaim to be AI-native without starting over
summary: Calendars hold more than just blocks of time. They reflect how people plan their days, coordinate with others, and make room for what matters to them. Reclaim, the Dropbox-owned calendar assistant, helps manage that complexity by using AI to find and adjust time for tasks, habits, and meetings. That approach works well when inputs and expected outcomes are clear. But people also use Reclaim for scheduling that’s less straightforward. As AI assistants and natural-language interfaces became more capable, they opened up a new way for people to use Reclaim. We imagined situations where users could describe a scheduling goal in their own words, even when it didn’t map neatly to an existing setting or command. Words alone wouldn’t be enough to determine what should happen on a real calendar, though. Reclaim still needs the context that gives requests meaning, including what’s already scheduled, when a user is available, and which preferences and commitments impact changes. Connecting natural-language requests with the surrounding calendar context could help people spend less time figuring out which settings or actions to use. But building the experience required more than adding an AI interface to the existing product. We needed to rethink how Reclaim turned conversational requests into calendar changes while preserving the scheduling system already in place. Evolving Reclaim for AI without starting over For our engineers, the rebuild started with the way Reclaim already managed calendars. Calendar changes carry real weight because time is precious and scheduled events often involve other people. Any new AI capability needed to feel like a natural extension of Reclaim, and it needed to work with the scheduling logic already in place. Before the redesign, Reclaim handled calendar changes in two primary ways. Users could make specific changes themselves, like moving an event or updating a setting. And Reclaim’s automated scheduler also worked in the background. It considered each person’s preferences and availability when finding time for tasks, focus work, and recurring routines like lunch, then adjusted those calendar blocks as schedules changed. The emergence of AI agents introduced a potential third way for users to use Reclaim. Instead of choosing a specific setting or command, a user might prefer to describe what they want to do in their own words. An agent could then interpret that request, look at the relevant parts of their calendar, and work out how Reclaim could help. But we needed to address several challenges before introducing agents to the experience. Large language models can interpret the same request in different ways because they generate answers based on patterns in their training data. For example, an open-ended request like “make time for this tomorrow” could lead an agent to find an open block, create a new event, or move something already on the calendar. Each option would affect the user’s schedule differently, and some could affect other people’s calendars, too. That variability made AI agents different from the two paths Reclaim already supported. Although they arrive at decisions differently, all three actors needed to rely on the same scheduling logic. Creating a separate AI-only path would have duplicated functionality and made Reclaim’s behavior harder to keep consistent across interfaces. We needed a system that could connect a model to both the right calendar information and Reclaim capabilities while also controlling how it used them. The result was an agent platform designed to work within Reclaim’s existing architecture. Building the agent platform Our agent platform gives a model relevant calendar details and access to Reclaim’s features while controlling what the model can see and do. The model interprets what the user says and figures out what they want. The agent, meanwhile, manages the larger process by providing Reclaim’s instructions, relevant calendar context, and tools (which let it ask Reclaim to look up information or request a specific action). When a tool returns information, the agent can send it back to the model to inform the next step. This repeated exchange is called the agent loop. As part of this process, Reclaim gives the agent the calendar information and tools relevant to each request, rather than access to everything at once. This helps the agent focus on the immediate task and limits it to the appropriate actions. For a more complex request, the agent can give one specific part to a specialized subagent. Internal checklists and review steps help keep the overall request on track. Ultimately, we opted to build the agent loop, tools, and the system for gathering context ourselves, and we connect directly to model providers instead of relying on a broad agent framework. That’s because a framework we initially explored lagged behind the provider APIs we wanted to use and included more structure than Reclaim needed. Owning these parts lets us design them around Reclaim’s scheduling needs, adopt new provider capabilities more quickly, and work with different model providers without rebuilding the rest of the platform. That leaves us with more code to maintain, though using agents to help with that code offsets some of the additional work. The same tool system supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) in two ways. Inside Reclaim’s agent loop, an MCP client lets the agent use compatible tools from other services. Separately, Reclaim’s MCP server makes selected Reclaim tools available through supported AI clients, including Claude and ChatGPT. Those clients use their own models and agent loops, but can call the same tools used within Reclaim. Our agent platform helped Reclaim work through open-ended requests, but we still needed safeguards around any changes it proposed. Users needed a way to review those changes before they reached their actual calendars. Making calendar changes consistent and reviewable Behind the scenes, Reclaim represents each scheduling capability as a Schedule Action, our internal term for a standard operation like creating or updating an event, changing an RSVP, or finding availability. Whether a request comes from a user, the automated scheduler, or an agent, the same Schedule Action type is used, including the same validation and commit process. That shared path matters because a calendar change can affect more than one event. Moving a meeting might change someone’s availability or cause Reclaim to adjust flexible events elsewhere on a user’s calendar. If each actor used a separate implementation, engineers would have to reproduce those rules and keep every version aligned as Reclaim evolved, which would have become tedious over time. Because all three actors use the same Schedule Action, engineers can change how an operation works in one place rather than updating three separate versions. This helps Reclaim behave consistently across its interfaces. But even when Reclaim handles a change consistently, users still need to see whether its wider effects match what they want to do. That’s why we developed Preview Mode, which gives users a temporary version of their calendar where they can review AI suggestions and changes requested through chat before applying them to their actual calendar. Essentially, they’re able to see how an event or settings change would affect the rest of their schedule before it goes live. They can then confirm that the change behaves as expected and review any effects on shared events before calendar updates are sent to other attendees. To keep Preview Mode fast, we reworked the automated scheduler as a pure function, meaning, in part, that it can calculate a proposed schedule without saving anything to the user’s actual calendar. Reclaim can repeat that calculation whenever the user adjusts the preview. Because busy calendars and meetings with several attendees require a lot of data, Reclaim keeps a readily accessible copy in Redis, a data store designed for fast retrieval. It also updates attendee availability within the preview whenever an event moves, so the next calculation reflects the schedule being proposed. Keeping AI workflows connected Reclaim now has a consistent path from a natural-language request to a reviewed calendar change. The agent platform connects models with relevant calendar information and Reclaim features, Schedule Actions route proposed updates through the product’s scheduling logic, and Preview Mode makes their effects visible before anything reaches the calendar or other attendees. Together, these pieces extend Reclaim with AI while preserving the scheduling experience people already rely on. This work also reinforced what AI needs in order to be useful inside an active workflow. A model needs the surrounding information to understand a request, a controlled way to act on it, and a review step before the result moves forward. In Reclaim, a scheduling goal can move from conversation to a proposed schedule and then to an approved calendar update without requiring the user to translate it into a specific setting or command. The long-term value of this rebuild is the freedom to evolve without fragmenting the product. As AI changes how people ask for help, Reclaim can introduce new capabilities through the same scheduling foundation rather than adding a separate experience each time. For Reclaim, this offers a practical framework for expanding AI-assisted workflows as models improve and people find new ways to manage their time. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Dropbox Tech] Dropbox CTO Ali Dasdan on moving from AI adoption to transformation
summary: As AI becomes a starting point for more kinds of work, its usefulness depends on access to an organization’s trusted knowledge and context, including the files, research, feedback, decisions, and project history that give the work meaning. Dropbox helps people bring that context into the supported AI tools they choose while preserving the permissions and controls they expect, so they can spend less time finding, uploading, and re-explaining what already exists. When AI helps them create something new, Dropbox gives that work a trusted, durable home where it can be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and built on over time. That focus on connected workflows also shapes how we use AI within Dropbox. Access to increasingly capable models can help teams produce more. But turning that output into sustained gains in productivity, quality, and customer impact requires examining workflows from end to end. That includes addressing new bottlenecks as output grows, adapting the platform that supports development, aligning organization-wide incentives, and measuring whether greater speed and volume lead to better outcomes. AI also increases the importance of human judgment. People still need to choose the right problems, give agents the context they need, evaluate the validity of their output, and remain in control of important decisions and actions. Problem solving, communication, and leadership become critical to turning AI-enabled output into real value. Dropbox Chief Technology Officer Ali Dasdan and Senior Director of Engineering Productivity Uma Namasivayam discuss lessons from deploying AI at company scale, how we assess productivity and ROI, how our progress compares with industry peers, and what organizations need to consider as they move from AI adoption to broader transformation. What have you learned in the last year about driving productivity with AI, not just for engineers but across the wider Dropbox organization? Ali: You have to start with the outcome you’re trying to achieve. Giving people AI tools is only the first step. As people use them, your assumptions get tested and new bottlenecks emerge. Maybe you’re coding faster, but now you have too many code reviews. Or you’re generating significantly more code, which puts additional stress on the tools and infrastructure that support development. If you want AI to have a meaningful impact, you have to look at the workflow end to end and keep adapting it until you’re producing the outcome you actually want. There’s no silver bullet. Uma: You have to approach it with a product mindset. Leadership saying, “You need to start using AI tools,” is good, but that alone won’t drive adoption. You also need ground-up awareness through initiatives like boot camps and show-and-tells that involve people more deeply. And you have to align incentives so managers understand what ROI they’re getting from it. How should companies think about measuring AI productivity and ROI? Ali: If I write 10 lines of code and push them to production, it’s almost impossible to prove those 10 lines were responsible for a certain amount of customer satisfaction or revenue improvement. I might produce a million lines a day, but if it’s the wrong product and customers have no interest in it, then it’s not going to work. The real ROI metrics are outcomes like revenue, cost, customer satisfaction, and retention. Then we look at proxy metrics that connect our output to those outcomes. Are we moving faster, producing more code, running more experiments, and pushing more features? Is the site faster and more reliable? There’s no single metric. The framework we use focuses on speed, effectiveness, quality, and impact, with multiple metrics under each. The industry hasn’t found the full solution yet. How does Dropbox’s AI-driven engineering productivity compare with companies operating at a similar level of technical scale and complexity? Ali: If we define peers as top technology companies we hire from and compete with for talent, we’re seeing very similar problems and metrics. We’re around 70% AI-generated code, and Uber recently shared a number around 70%. They see a need for internal agentic coding solutions, and so do we. They have their own tools, and we have Nova, our internal service for running coding agents. Larger companies have allocated more resources to these problems, while we’re super lean. Despite that, I feel like we’re comparable with that peer group across multiple metrics, including how quickly we adopted AI and reached our targets. Compared with the broader industry, it appears we’re ahead. Uma: The industry looks at pull request throughput, or the rate at which teams complete code changes, as one proxy metric for productivity. It’s not ‌perfect, but our throughput ranks in the top 5% in a custom benchmark of companies with similarly large, complex codebases and engineering systems. We also look at whether moving faster affects quality. Our change failure percentage, which measures how often a deployment leads to degraded performance or failure, is in line with industry peers at the 75th percentile. Our token usage is also among the lowest in that peer group, which could indicate that our teams or systems are operating efficiently. Together, these measures give us a fuller picture of how we’re doing against similar companies. As AI usage grows, how do you decide where additional investment is worthwhile? Ali: AI requires money, and when we talk about AI funding, we’re talking about a large portfolio. There are products used by individual functions, capabilities in tools like Zoom and Slack, company-wide deployments like ChatGPT Enterprise, automation tools, and coding models. We’re seeing benefits. People are fixing tech debt, long-running migration projects are getting finished, and we’re delivering most of the roadmap with fewer resources. But organizations still have to decide which ideas to pursue and when to invest more, often before they can draw a direct line to ROI. That requires domain expertise, the right incentives, and a lot of judgment. We’re still working through it along with the rest of the industry. How should companies determine whether their AI spend is creating real value? Ali: At Dropbox, we’re starting to think less about raw token consumption and more about the engineering value those tokens create. With Nova, for example, we can connect agent usage to actual engineering workflows, validation, and outcomes. That gives us a way to evaluate AI spend based on the engineering work those tokens help produce, rather than simply how many tokens we’re consuming. As AI lowers the cost and effort required to produce software, which human skills become more valuable? Ali: If you look fundamentally at what engineers or computer scientists do, it’s that we know how to solve a problem. That’ll never disappear. AI may help me solve bigger problems or solve them faster, but I still need to provide better context, ask the right questions, judge the validity of the answers, know how to iterate, and give a good spec and problem definition. I also need to understand how a solution fits into the broader system and adapt as the tools change. Problem solving, communication, systems thinking, and judgment become even more important because agents depend on people to guide and evaluate their work. Uma: I would give you three things. One is problem solving, which Ali explained really well. The second is judgment. The next phase of AI could make the cost of engineering almost zero, which makes choosing the right problems and evaluating what AI produces extremely important. The third is leadership. Leaders need to understand people, navigate ambiguity as work changes, bring teams together, communicate clearly, build trust, and make sure incentives are aligned. Those skills won’t go away at all. Their value will only grow. As AI models and agents become more widely available, what’ll distinguish the organizations that use them effectively, and what role can Dropbox play? Ali: Models and agents can be incredibly capable, but they don’t automatically know which information an organization trusts, what decisions have already been made, who has access, or what needs to happen next. Without that context, even a strong model can produce generic or incomplete results. Dropbox can connect supported AI experiences to customer-owned content and context, then give the work AI produces a place to be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and continued. People still make consequential decisions, while the work keeps moving without losing the sources, history, and collaborators behind it. A year from now, what do you hope AI-enabled work looks like at Dropbox? Uma: This year, we’ve focused heavily on engineering, and we’re now starting to understand the workflows across product, design, and other non-engineering teams. A year from now, the goal is for people across those teams to be able to come up with ideas, test them with customers, and potentially ship some of those features. If our customer experience team sees an issue, for example, they could use agents to develop a solution and see whether it works for the customer. That’s the vision we’re pursuing internally. If we can prove it works, we could potentially enable external customers to build on Dropbox platforms and use AI with the building blocks we have. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Docker] Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist
summary: This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line. Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed. This story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline. This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media. Today’s Horror Story: The Review That Made Everything Up A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change. He named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name. What made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is company source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously. He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built. The version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice. The change he pushed that night His product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known issues go away. So he bumped the version. - POSTGRES_VERSION=16.11 + POSTGRES_VERSION=16.13 This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters. What came back BuaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two. The report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the new PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party company, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist. It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem. Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch. And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing. In this issue, you’ll learn: Why a read-only agent that only writes comments can still get your cluster taken down What makes a fabricated security finding harder to dismiss than an obviously broken one Why agent output belongs in the untrusted column, the same as agent input How to move a real AI code reviewer into a Docker Sandbox, step by step, and what that does and does not protect you from Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it. The Problem It is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more. The trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could. This engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to. What makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report. How Docker Sandboxes Contain This Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists. Remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a new teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work. Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have. That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it. This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person. Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory. How BuaJi runs today BuaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script. The script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log. The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything. What we want instead We split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else. One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out. Step 1: Let BuaJi find Ollama somewhere other than localhost Inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default: - url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" + base = os.environ.get("OLLAMA_URL", "http://localhost:11434") + url = f"{base}/api/generate" Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner. Step 2: Bake BuaJi’s dependencies into a sandbox image, once Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time. Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything: FROM docker/sandbox-templates:shell USER root RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-requests git \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* USER agent Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE. Step 3: Keep the model on the runner Ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline. ollama serve > /tmp/ollama.log 2>&1 & sleep 2 ollama pull "$LLM" The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5. Step 4: Create the sandbox with the code mounted read-only This step decides what BuaJi can see and change. mkdir -p "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" sbx run -d --name "$SBX_NAME" -t "$BUAJI_TEMPLATE" \ shell "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" "$CI_PROJECT_DIR:ro" Here is what each part does: --name gives each pipeline its own sandbox. -t uses the image from Step 2. shell is the agent type. BuaJi is a plain script, so a shell sandbox is enough. buaji-scratch is an empty folder, the only place BuaJi can write. :ro mounts the repository read-only. BuaJi can read files and run git diff, but cannot change anything. Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with. Step 5: Open one network path, to the model Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.) sbx policy allow network --sandbox "$SBX_NAME" localhost:11434 The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port, the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have. Step 6: Run the review BuaJi runs as before, just in a new place with only two variables: sbx exec -w "$CI_PROJECT_DIR" \ -e LLM="$LLM" \ -e OLLAMA_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434 \ "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" python3 buaji.py | tee buaji-review.log -w starts in the checkout, where buaji.py expects rules.md. The two -e flags are the only variables BuaJi can see. tee saves the review to a file on the runner, outside the sandbox. The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next. Step 7: Check every CVE number before anyone acts on the report This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it. It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist: unverified="" for id in $(grep -oE 'CVE-{4}-{4,}' buaji-review.log | sort -u); do count=$(curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=$id" \ | jq -r '.totalResults // 0')  && unverified="$unverified $id" done if ; then echo "⚠️ BuaJi output mentions CVE IDs that do not exist:$unverified" echo "⚠️ Treat this review as unverified. Do not run any commands it suggests." exit 1 fi Because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it.. It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together. Step 8: Check what BuaJi tried to reach, then clean up Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox: sbx policy log "$SBX_NAME" sbx stop "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" sbx rm -f "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" The log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at. Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean. The complete pipeline job Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this: # BuaJi, moved into a Docker Sandbox. The read-only rule is now a property of # the environment, not a convention in the script: the code is mounted :ro, no # credentials are passed in, and only one network path (to the model) is open. buaji: stage: buaji tags: - self-hosted-gpu-kvm # GPU for Ollama, KVM for sbx microVMs variables: LLM: gemma GIT_DEPTH: "2" # buaji.py diffs HEAD^ against HEAD SBX_NAME: buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID before_script: - ollama serve > /tmp/ollama.log 2>&1 & - sleep 2 - ollama pull "$LLM" - mkdir -p "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" - sbx run -d --name "$SBX_NAME" -t "$BUAJI_TEMPLATE" shell "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" "$CI_PROJECT_DIR:ro" - sbx policy allow network --sandbox "$SBX_NAME" localhost:11434 script: - sbx exec -w "$CI_PROJECT_DIR" -e LLM="$LLM" -e OLLAMA_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434 "$SBX_NAME" python3 buaji.py | tee buaji-review.log - ./scripts/verify-cves.sh buaji-review.log after_script: - sbx policy log "$SBX_NAME" - sbx stop "$SBX_NAME" && sbx rm -f "$SBX_NAME" allow_failure: true only: changes: - "**/*.go" The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails. What changed Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out. What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them. Best Practices Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself. Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember. Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet. Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6. Clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism. Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them. Conclusion The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it. Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster. As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

title: [Docker] PHP2Shell and eMudhra Patched
summary: Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Both reached the same place, the foundation their applications are built on. PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They let an unauthenticated request become code execution on the server, on any PHP application, however careful its own code is, and PHP runs about 69% of the websites whose server-side language is known. The eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem. Eight intermediate certificates from the certificate authority eMudhra turned out to have private keys that can be computed from the public certificates, which let anyone issue a certificate for any website and have it accepted. Browsers revoke certificates like these on their own, but a container image carries its own trust store and keeps trusting them until it is rebuilt. Docker Hardened Images published a fixed PHP image within 24 hours The dhi.io/php image was rebuilt on the patched PHP and published early on October 22, within 24 hours of the upstream release and after the DHI testing and verification steps. Pulling the current tag puts you on the fixed version. The few DHI images that bundle their own PHP application, such as composer and nextcloud, follow as their upstream projects release. Rebuilt across the catalog, verifiable tag by tag The certificate compromise touched the whole catalog, because every image carries a trust store. In the 48 hours after the PHP release, the DHI build system ran 16,567 package and image builds across the catalog. By 10pm UTC on October 22, almost all catalog tags were on the fixed CA store, with most of the rest in the build queue. That percentage comes from the SBOM that ships with every image, read for every published tag to check which CA store and which PHP version it carries, and you can run the same check on anything you pull. How to make sure your environments are covered If you run PHP on Docker Hardened Images, pull the current tag for your branch and redeploy, and rebuild anything you built on top of a DHI image so it picks up the new base docker pull dhi.io/php:8.4 Customizations built through the DHI Enterprise workflow are rebuilt automatically when the base layer is patched. For the certificate fix the same applies to every image you build from a DHI base, PHP or not. The Docker Security update from October 22 lists the affected PHP versions and the support path. If you run PHP in any other container, check the PHP version running inside it rather than the tag on the outside, and rebuild it on a patched base. Build from a trusted foundation Weeks like this one will keep coming, but a trusted foundation will make all the difference. If you are not building on hardened images yet, this week is the wake-up call and the week to start. Both events landed on the foundation, and that is where the fix has to happen, in the image itself, rebuilt from fixed sources before anyone pulls it. This is exactly what Docker Hardened Images were built for. Docker builds, patches and maintains the system packages inside each image from source, and the build system is event-driven, so an upstream release or a changed package triggers rebuilds of everything that depends on it. Each image ships signed, with its SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance and VEX data attached, which is why a rebuild of this size can be measured as well as done. The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with near-zero CVEs on every image. It stays compatible with the Alpine and Debian your teams already run, so adoption is a one-line change to the FROM line in your Dockerfile, with no migration project attached. DHI Select and DHI Enterprise add SLA-backed remediation with critical CVE fixes within 7 days, FIPS and STIG variants, image customization with the guarantees kept, and Extended Lifecycle Support for the versions upstream has stopped patching. All of it is in the Docker Hardened Images catalog, free to pull today.

title: [Sentry] Finding performance wins in our own traces with a coding agent
summary: For the last few weeks I've used a coding agent to find and fix backend performance issues in Sentry, starting from the traces Sentry sends to itself. Most of the fixes only changed a line or two. But together, they removed hundreds of millions of queries a week, and some expensive lookups became hundreds or thousands of times faster (more details on that below). Pointing the agent at our traces I connected my agent (in this case Claude with Opus 5.5) to the Sentry MCP, pointed it at our own Sentry org and project, and asked it to find hot code path issues similar to a small performance PR I had drafted: use the sentry mcp to look for more similar quick wins around hot path issues things With the latest few model releases, I've found that you don't have to be as specific with how you structure prompts, or make sure that you're controlling context for the agent (for example sharing specific example spans). You can start with something as general as: Find all the critical paths in my application. Use the sentry MCP to find their traces and find ways to optimize them. Based on my initial prompt, the agent sorted spans by how often they ran and how long they took. For each candidate it gave me a file and line, an estimated weekly volume, and a link to an example trace. When the list got thin, I'd point it somewhere new. My prompts were short and mostly questions like: "look for database heavy issues" "is this change risky in any way?" "did you validate the new query using EXPLAIN like we did earlier" "rpc might also be interesting" "i think there's a pr from someone that might already fix this" "lets not touch that area" Then I'd pick an issue and have it investigate further before changing anything. It read the code and the git history and told me what might break. If the fix held up, it opened a draft PR. Sentry is a large codebase, and there are areas I don't know well enough to change confidently. I'd steer the agent away from those, check for work already in progress, and keep looking for something smaller. Making sure the agent has the ability to validate changes in the read-only database rather than guessing leads to much better results. Django SDK instrumentation as a starting point A lot of the Sentry codebase is in Django, and the Sentry Django SDK's automatic instrumentation gave us a good starting point: Django query spans include the SQL as their description. Our traces also include cache calls, cross-silo RPCs, tasks, and API routes. Grouping spans by description gave the agent a way to turn trace data into a ranked list of expensive work. When query-source attributes were available on a database span, they gave the agent the file and line that ran the query. The user_agent attribute showed that one busy endpoint was mostly sentry-cli set-commits --auto paging through an org's repositories on every build. One org had ~16k repositories and was doing this roughly every 40 seconds. That led to a CLI change to avoid the pagination and a server-side index to make the queries cheaper for existing CLI versions. Every PR links an example trace showing the extra query or call, so that it's a bit easier for a reviewer to understand. In one trace, a webhook ran the same 140ms query twice. The result from removing a query was easy to see in a trace. To find out how much it mattered, I also checked request latency and database load in Sentry. Checking query changes For SQL changes, the agent ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after on a read-only database mirror and compared the results. The clearest query cleanup was GroupHistory lookup (GroupHistory records each status change on an issue). The query asked for the newest row across several statuses, meaning Postgres read and sorted every matching row: -- before SELECT * FROM sentry_grouphistory WHERE group_id = %s AND status IN (1, 2, 11, 12, 13) ORDER BY date_added DESC LIMIT 1 -- after: one probe per status, take the max in Python (SELECT date_added FROM sentry_grouphistory WHERE group_id = %s AND status = 1 ORDER BY date_added DESC LIMIT 1) UNION ALL ... For the busiest group on the mirror this went from 935ms to 0.4ms with a warm cache. Results Check that the property exists on the event before running the query during event ingestion. That UPDATE was running ~10k/s on the attachments database in our US region and is now basically gone. Commits on that database fell ~17%, and link_event_to_user_report averaged ~6ms → ~2.5ms. Reuse the already loaded project and skip unnecessary lookups in two hot paths. Reusing the project removed an estimated ~143M extra SELECTs a week. Together, the two occurrence-ingestion fixes brought save_issue_occurrence p50 from ~35ms to ~30ms and p95 from ~95ms to ~61ms versus the same hours the previous day (detector lookup fix). Rearrange the GroupHistory query to use the existing index more efficiently when updating issue status. That query accounted for ~8% of disk reads on the primary database in our EU (Germany) region and ~3% in our US region, and its disk reads fell to nearly zero. Status changes in the occurrence consumer were ~30% faster in the US region and ~13% faster in the EU region versus the same time the previous day. Eager-load the application and token for Sentry app requests to skip round trips later. The two extra selects went from ~1.9% of query volume on the control database to ~0.16%. That works out to roughly 29M fewer queries a day. The fix joins the related objects into two queries we're already making. Add a missing table index for repository pagination. The paginated query alone accounted for ~1.6% of query execution time on the primary database in our US region before rollout. Average database execution fell ~69% (30ms → 9.2ms), with ~52% fewer cached block accesses per query. Requests weren't consistently faster, but they did less database work. Call bulk_set once instead of setting the cache once per issue in results, to reduce round trips. Writing the unhandled flag used to take one cache round trip per issue, about 51ms in the measured example. Batching those writes took one round trip and about 1.2ms. Work around poor Postgres planner performance for a query in detectors. On the database mirror, a query for a small detector fell from 180ms to 0.2ms with a warm cache. Note: Query volumes and daily savings are estimates based on sampled spans and observed traffic. I compared database work per request or query so changes in traffic wouldn't be misrepresented as performance improvements. Trying it on your own app To get started: If you don't already use Sentry, sign up for Sentry Give your coding agent access to the Sentry MCP Prompt your agent to find performance issues in your app. You can start generally and work down to specific areas like: "Find transactions where the same query, with different parameters, runs more than 10 times in a single trace (N+1)." "Find SELECT * or wide queries on hot paths where only a few columns are used." "Find slow queries with ORDER BY ... LIMIT, OFFSET pagination, or LIKE '%...' that likely aren't using an index." Pick an issue and have it investigate further before changing anything. Have it read the code and the git history and assess what might break. Then open a PR. You can also use natural language queries in the Sentry UI's Explore tabs for Logs, Traces, and Metrics to ask things like "Which database queries had the highest P95 duration over the last 7 days?"

title: [Engineering at Meta] F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
summary: Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020. F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline. This post introduces F3 Lightning, an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently. The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access. With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period. A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results. The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request. F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes. Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph. Figure 1: F3 consolidates all features into one merged graph. The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph. Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production. Figure 2: One failing feature blocks the entire release. Failures became more frequent as F3 scaled. F3 originally served a few hundred features, and at that size merges succeeded and releases were largely smooth. Today that number is more than 20,000, and different feature types need their own checks depending on how they compute, so new features and modified features are held to different testing bars. A feature that a model already consumes needs model-related tests before it can be released. Those tests are computationally expensive enough that they run only in a later release stage, and, because the merged graph ships as one unit, every other feature in it waits for them too. F3 Lightning: Making Each Feature Its Own Release and Sharing Computation After F3 launched, we made several rounds of improvements to the merged graph. Each one brought back release speed for a while, but the gains eroded as more features landed, because all features still shipped together in the merged graph. So F3 Lightning was built to make every feature releasable on its own while preserving F3’s efficiency. As illustrated in Figure 3, F3 Lightning introduced two changes to help achieve this: Deployment granularity: Each feature is an independently releasable configuration. It is validated, shipped, and rolled back without affecting any other feature. Efficiency parity: F3’s efficiency came from the merged graph, so giving every feature its own release removes the source of it. Matching that efficiency while keeping per-feature releases required several key optimizations in how F3 Lightning executes. Figure 3: F3 Lightning separates the release boundary from the execution boundary. Deployment Granularity: How F3 Lightning Isolates Feature Releases Isolation starts in the compiler, where each feature is compiled on its own into a single configuration. That feature configuration carries everything needed to extract that feature — every node it needs, in order, with nothing borrowed from a neighbor. If feature C has a problem, feature A still ships, because the two configurations have no relationship to each other. Figure 4: A bad feature no longer blocks a good one. Because features are no longer merged at release time, each one can be selected and released on its own schedule. The release path becomes an ordered queue instead of a batch that ships all at once or not at all. Changes are prioritized by what they unblock. A new feature that no model consumes yet can go out quickly on standard validation, while a change to a feature a live model already reads gets extra testing first. Figure 5: Features are selected from a priority queue by impact and risk. Efficiency Parity: How F3 Lightning Preserved F3’s Serving Efficiency Our first prototypes separated deployment only. Features shipped independently, but execution was no longer shared, so the prototypes used substantially more CPU than traditional F3. Each independently released configuration arrived at the serving process as its own graph and was executed separately, repeating every read, filter, and aggregation that F3’s merged graph had eliminated. The fix was to bring shared execution back without bringing the merge back. At startup, F3 Lightning does not rebuild a merged graph. It takes the active feature configurations, consolidates the work they share, and arranges it into a single execution order. Getting back to parity took four steps: a compiler prerequisite followed by three startup optimizations. Step 1: Stable Identifiers Make Shared Work Recognizable To deduplicate execution, the runtime must recognize when two independently compiled configurations contain the same computation. Node numbers can’t do this, because numbering is local to each feature’s graph. The same seven-day filter might be node 2 in one configuration and node 7 in another, and inserting a single node renumbers everything after it. Traditional F3 never had this problem, because one compiler run saw every feature and could assign identifiers globally. F3 Lightning instead has the compiler derive each identifier from what the work does, not where it sits: the operation, its parameters, and the identifiers of its inputs (see Figure 6). Because each input’s identifier already reflects everything upstream of it, the identifier captures the whole chain of work that produced the result. Where input order doesn’t affect the result, inputs are put in a standard order. Aggregations also include the properties that define their behavior, such as the time window and grouping keys. As a result, two features that define the same operation over the same inputs receive the same identifier, even if they were compiled and released weeks apart. If a computation’s meaning changes, its identifier changes with it. Figure 6: The same computation gets the same identifier. Step 2: One Execution Plan Across Every Feature At service startup, F3 Lightning builds a single execution plan across all active features, using a topological sort to place every node after the nodes it depends on. When several features contain a node with the same identifier, the plan keeps one copy and connects every consumer to it, so that computation runs once no matter how many features use it. Merging guarantees each computation runs once, but the plan is still a graph that the executor walks pointer by pointer on every request. The same startup pass therefore flattens it into an ordered list, so each request runs a single forward pass down the list instead of traversing a graph. Sharing one plan raises a risk: A single failing computation could affect every feature. To prevent this, if a computation fails or its input is unavailable, F3 Lightning marks everything downstream of it as not ready, and the executor skips that work. A failure affects only the nodes that depend on it, and independent branches keep running. Step 3: A Shared Memory Buffer, Because Deduplication Was Not Enough After steps 1 and 2 were complete, no computation ran twice, yet CPU use was still above traditional F3. The remaining compute cost came from memory layout. Each configuration carried its own request-time data container, so intermediate results were scattered across separate memory allocations. Walking the plan in order meant jumping between them, and each jump cost a cache miss. F3 Lightning replaced those per-feature containers with one buffer per request. At startup, each feature’s references are rebound to slots in that buffer. Three improvements follow from the single buffer: Locality: Consecutive plan steps now touch adjacent memory, so the values a step reads are usually already in cache. This restores the sequential access pattern the merged graph always had. It also removes the per-feature allocation on every request. One readiness vector: A single vector, stored apart from the values, replaces per-feature tracking, so the executor can check whether a value is ready without reading the value itself. The marker has to be separate because an empty list is a valid result, so “empty” can’t also mean “not computed yet.” No duplicate copies: Most feature values are lists and maps, and consumers no longer get their own copy. The shared slot holds a reference to the producer’s result, so a computation used by 20 features is computed once and stored once. Single values (scalars) are still copied, because copying a small value is cheaper than following a pointer. This is safe because each buffer lasts only for one request, and the execution order guarantees each result outlives its last reader. Figure 8: All features share one memory buffer. Step 4: Dense Index Mapping Removes the Last Per-Access Cost Values now lived together, but finding one was still computationally expensive. Every access had to resolve an identifier, which meant hashing a key, probing buckets, and following a pointer. Lookups weren’t computationally efficient at Meta’s serving volume. The final fix applied the same principle as steps 2 and 3, doing the work once at startup. F3 Lightning assigns every unique identifier a consecutive integer slot and rewrites every reference in every configuration to point at those slots, so identifiers are used only during initialization. Reading a result becomes a direct array index into the shared buffer, with no hashing and no lookup table on the request path. With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than on traditional F3, with no increase in infrastructure computational cost. That shorter release cycle means models can be improved and retrained more often in the same period. Building F3 Lightning also taught us three lessons: Deployment and execution should have separate boundaries: If one artifact determines both how components run and when they ship, a failure in any one of them blocks all the others. Splitting the two jobs removed a trade-off between efficiency and release speed. Work that never changes between requests belongs at startup, not on the request path: Three tasks were identical for every request: spotting shared work, deciding the order to run it in, and finding where each result is stored. F3 Lightning now does them once, when the service starts, so independent releases add no computational cost to individual requests. Two designs can execute the same operations in the same order and still differ substantially in CPU computational cost: In F3 Lightning, we removed every repeated computation, yet CPU use stayed above traditional F3. Each feature still kept its own copy of the shared results, spread across memory. Consolidating them into one copy per result closed the gap. This is the least obvious result in the project and the one that generalizes furthest. On modern CPUs, where results live and how many copies exist can matter as much as how many computations run.
